utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today, we are the 14th of May, 2008. I would like to greet all the people present in the courtroom. I would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us. Before we resume the witness's testimony, I would like to mention that before coming to this hearing, I checked whether the website of the Tribunal was working properly. Well, in fact, it is not working properly. According to the Registry, the company, a Dutch company, that transmits images has a technical problem at the moment. This is how things stand. Today, at two minutes -- 14 hours, 59 minutes and 47 seconds. I hope that we will soon be able to identify what the problem is and find a solution. Are there any housekeeping matters which you would like to address. The Prosecution? No. Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing, except to inform you that yesterday I received from the Prosecution information about the documents disclosed with respect to Witness Riedlmayer, but it doesn't say there whether that's all the material that should be disclosed to me, because they list what has been disclosed so far. I'm not sure that that is the complete set, because Witness Riedlmayer testified in the Milutinovic trial, Milosevic trial, the Krajisnik trial according to information that I received, and I assume that he also testified in the Martic trial, whereas I don't have those documents. If he did testify, that's fine, but it doesn't say that the disclosure process has been completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, we addressed this issue, and I would like to ask the Prosecution to disclose to the accused all the transcripts of the trials in which he has testified. You told us that this had been done, but it hasn't been done, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to Your Honours and everyone in and around the courtroom. I believe that we have, in fact, disclosed all of the transcripts from the prior testimony of Dr. Riedlmayer. I'm aware that there might be a small amount of Rule 68 material that will be disclosed to Dr. Seselj, but my understanding is that all transcripts of his prior testimony have, in fact, been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's bring the witness in. I believe that the Prosecution has five to ten minutes left. Mr. Mussemeyer, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Depends a bit on the answers of the witness, but I have only three questions left and one document which I intend to introduce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, clearly the following witness -- as far as the following witness is concerned, we won't have time to finish this witness tomorrow, so he will have to stay over the weekend and we will have to hear him next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we're not able to finish him, then obviously, yes, Mr. President, he would have to continue into next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give the floor back to the Prosecution, who has a few questions to put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: First of all, Madam Registrar, I would like to have 65 ter number 800 on the monitor, and I would ask the witness to look at this document and if he can comment about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in, please, so that I can see it better? Can I see the rest of the page, please? It's very hard to decipher. Could you just ... Yes. This is a list of refugees from Vocin who came to Slatina on the 14th and 15th of December, 1991, and who were put up with various families in Slatina and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to have this document moved into evidence. And for the complete information of your Judges, this exhibit has been tendered in the Milosevic case as Exhibit number 334, tab 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, what is the provenance of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You mean the source where we got it from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The source, the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: According to our documentation, it was submitted by the US representative McCloskey, Frank. The submission date is unknown, but the date of the document is the 15th of December, 1991. This is what I can give you as information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you confirm that there were refugees from Vocin who went to Slatina? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I know some of them personally, and the document was probably compiled by the Red Cross, those people in the Red Cross who took over the refugees and put them up with the families, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness is saying "probably" here. Now, if he says "probably," that doesn't mean a thing. We received the document, and the Prosecutor subsequently told us in the court that he received it from some American representative by the name of McCloskey, which also means nothing. Perhaps the facts on this document are completely in order and correct, but we cannot accept the document because we don't know whose it is. It's got nothing official on it, and you can barely read the title, either. We don't know who compiled it, and nothing else is known about it either. So I think it is impossible to admit that kind of document into evidence. And you can see that somebody, in handwriting, put corrections to those names. We don't know if the names are correct, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will deliberate on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, McCloskey, who is a US representative, who is this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I cannot give you detailed information about this. I only know the name, and I know that he was a representative from the US, but I don't have further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will give an MFI number to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P434, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more thing that I'd like to draw your attention to. In the heading, it says: "Refugees from Vocin." You can discern that, but the question remains whether I read it out correctly. Then you can't read the next word, and then it says: "The 14th and 15th of December," which is the time when Vocin was falling into Croatian hands, when, in fact, the Serbs started fleeing from Western Slavonia en masse, in their masses, and then the Croats were fleeing, but on the opposite side. So what kind of refugees are these? Are these refugees that fled from Serb forces or in the face of Croatian forces? This is so tendentious and the whole thing is so suspect that you really can't make head or tail. You see it says "14th and 15th of December," there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is why this document has an MFI number. So as things stand, this document has not been admitted. Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, I come to the last issue. This deals with the refugees from Vojvodina. Do you know if refugees from Serbs arrived from Western Slavonia and when?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The refugees from Vojvodina started arriving into the area of the former Slatina Municipality and the county, as it was later called, at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, and the process continued. Several hundred families arrived in our area from the villages of Beska, Slankamen, and villages around Ruma and Sid, and the reason for their arrival was there was pressure exerted upon them over there to force them to leave their homes, to have their houses exchanged, and, in fact, to move out of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these refugees?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were exclusively Croats, ethnic Croats, and according to their own statements, the pressures exerted upon them were done by members of the Serbian Radical Party. What they did was to threaten them by calling them up and demanding that they move out. Then they would throw bombs into their gardens and yards. They applied all forms of coercion to instill fear into them so that the process of exchanging homes and their departure to Croatia should start and be a continuous process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Where do you know this from? Did you talk to them?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we talked to them, and they even published a book about it, about all those events and the traumas they went through, and how they made due in their new environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was my last question. I have additional information for you related to the documents from yesterday and the videos. If you wanted to hear this from me, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: We discussed yesterday about this video, the destruction of the church in Vocin. We are now in a position -- we have the same complete video clip, and we have subtitles, because Judge Harhoff asked us to have the translation ready, and we have it subtitled. We can play it in the courtroom, if you wish to hear this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time will this take?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The tape is 18 seconds' long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think if it's 18 seconds, we can listen to this. So, please, let's hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 18 seconds go by very quickly. Perhaps you should show it to us again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I've been recording since 7.00. You're nowhere to be found. Why don't you go in front, then record the front then the back."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This was a bit longer, and I think this is the one which we wanted to show you. Mr. Seselj was opposing that we cut it at the White Eagles, and now we have it complete here. We also have it also in written. If you need this, I can, with the help of the usher, give it to you. The second information I can give you: There was a question about monitoring people, because some of them were speaking French. I checked this and found out that it was not the UN who made this observation, it was the EU Monitoring -- it was people from the EU who monitored this, and we are in the possession of reports, but these reports are very general. If you need, I can give you the ERN numbers for these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That won't be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So my last question will be to have these video clips moved into evidence, and I must do one short correction for the last video we saw about the destruction of the church. It is from 65 ter number 6044, and the ERN number is V000-2916. Instead the other two video are from 65 ter number 468.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have exhibit numbers for the two video clips, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are three video clips, all in all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first video will become Exhibit P435. The second video will become P436, and the third video that we saw today will become Exhibit P437.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I finish my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before I give the floor to Mr. Seselj, I have a question for you. I thought the Prosecution would have put you the question, but they didn't. I would like to come back to the attack on the village of Cetekovac. This was on the 14th of September, 1991. You said that this was done by paramilitaries who were headed by Boro Lukic, a former captain from the JNA. You mentioned that an investigation had been carried out and that the reports had been sent to the prosecutor who was dealing with the matter. As far as you know, do you know whether there was a trial after that and that Boro Lukic was indicted? What happened to him; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said yesterday, the event occurred on the 4th of September, 1991, with all the details that I described, and it ended up in a criminal report being filed against Boro Lukic and the rest who took part in that terrible massacre. The criminal report was sent to the District Prosecutor's Office in Osijek, and then it was passed over to Bjelovar. Investigations were undertaken, and as far as I know, some of the perpetrators, who were identified during the investigation later and confirmed to be the perpetrators, they were tried in absentia. Now, what happened to Boro Lukic, he left with his unit to Bosnia first, and then later on, according to my information, he ended up in Serbia, and I have no further knowledge of him after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seemingly, there was a trial in absentia. Mr. Prosecutor, did you know that a trial had been conducted against the attackers of Cetekovac?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: No, I have no further information about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this person called "Boro Lukic ," did you never hear any more about him? You don't know what's become of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where he is or what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned this trial, and you said that some of the people were prosecuted in absentia. Among the accused were those people were prosecuted, was there Boro Lukic as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly whether he was found guilty in his absence or if the trial is still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have two hours for your cross-examination, so you may start.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, I hope that yesterday you understood what the main problem in your testimony is, as far as I'm concerned, with respect to the last remark I made to the Prosecutor. You said here yesterday that the massacre of the civilians in Vocin was committed by the White Eagles and Seselj's men, and you quoted a figure of about 80. Now, in your statement, the one you gave to the Prosecutor in 2002, you state, and I'm going could quote that portion: "In the night between the 12th and 13th of December, 1991, the Serb forces, when they were withdrawing, massacred 43 civilians in Vocin. The massacre was perpetrated by a paramilitary unit from Serbia called the White Eagles." There is no mention of Seselj's men there, just as there is no mention of them in your statement as a whole. Who proposed that you involve Seselj's men or, rather, the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party who some people called "Seselj's men" into this statement, who told you to put it in?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a statement from -- my statement from 2002, where the term or phrase "White Eagles" was used, and under that name, in the territory of Vocin and further afield, there was the paramilitary unit of volunteers from Serbia, and they were the White Eagles, members of the Serbian Radical Party, Seselj's men, volunteers who perhaps were not in some other unit, but they were in the same locations, under the same command, and as I said yesterday, the perception of them, according to the victims and refugees and population and witnesses who provided testimony, they always used the term "White Eagles." That's the term that was used. So these were people who had come from Serbia and who took part in that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't question that. I'm not challenging that at all, because I spoke about that in Serbia before I came to The Hague. But how come suddenly, when we come to this specific crime, that you mention the White Eagles and Seselj's men, because yesterday, when you referred to volunteers from Serbia, you said that some of them were called "the White Eagles," some of them were referred to as volunteers from Serbia, and others were "Seselj's men," and in one place you say that the White Eagles arrived with Colonel Trbojevic to Western Slavonia. I think you made a mistake there, too, and I'll tell you what my information and knowledge is about that. And this information has already been presented in the court here, so you can tell me your position in the matter. According to a statement made by Colonel Trbojevic, at his initiative, a unit of volunteers arrived through the Territorial Defence of Novi Sad, led by Captain Jovan Kulic. So those are the volunteers from Serbia, in the narrow sense. There were so-called Seselj's men. They were volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. There were over 600 of them, and perhaps at one point there might have been 700 of them. I don't challenge that at all. And then you had the White Eagles as well. Perhaps this figure of 80 is exaggerated. To the best of my knowledge, there are about 50 of them. So I'm not challenging any of that, I'm not disputing that. All I am disputing or challenging is the fact that you subsequently introduced, among the actors of the crime, the perpetrators of the crime in Vocin, Seselj's men, Seseljevci. So do you have any proof or evidence to show that even one volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party took part in the crime in Vocin, a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party, and not going by what people's perceptions of them were and who called them what, because I assume that victims could not have specifically differentiated between one or another formation or unit, but you, as a policeman, as a police inspector holding a high rank, were probably able to make that distinction?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated yesterday, there are numerous witness statements and statements by victims, by refugees, those survived the crime. It is precisely that information that was used in our crime investigation. That night, during the night when this crime was committed, when these 60 or so criminals were actually on rampage in Vocin and massacring and killing people, the people saw that this was being done by these volunteers from Serbia and by the locals whom they used to see all the time throughout the months and days of the occupation. So this is based -- the crime investigation data is based on the statements of eyewitnesses who had gone through that massacre and all the atrocities in Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please, could you specify what part of the declaration you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... when Mladen Kulic was testifying, Jovan Kulic was mentioned at that time. The criminal report of the Banja Luka Court of against Mladen Kulic and another number of volunteers from Novi Sad was being shown at that time. I presented a statement of Jovan Trbojevic who said how Jovan Kulic came to Western Slavonia. My thesis was that Jovan Kulic was not a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party, either. If you remember, the OTP showed that criminal complaint on the screen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, we agree about a certain figure, namely, that there were around 600 volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party there. Yesterday, you stated that it was in that number that those volunteers also left on buses. Do you remember having said that? And you also said that a group remained -- you first said about 70 and then about 80 in Vocin and that group perpetrated the massacre. Towards the end of your testimony yesterday, you said that it was the White Eagles and the Seselj's men. If there was 600 people who were volunteers of Seselj's party -- I don't like this name, "Seselj's men," because these are not just blind adherence to a personal policy of mine, but these are volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, so they are followers of party ideas, not mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, there are a number of problems with the translation. Could you please slow down, because you are speaking so fast that understandably interpreters might make mistakes. So please slow down, especially when you're dealing with the issues which are of importance to you. So please speak slowly. That way, the risk of mistakes is then null.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to take this opportunity to say that my contribution was misinterpreted. I speak slowly, and there was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 24, page 13, I did not ask which section of the statement. I said, "What statement were you referring to, Mr. Seselj?" Thank you for correcting what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please move on, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The mistake was in the transcript only because I heard it correctly. I heard your question correctly, and I think that I directly answered your question, Judge Lattanzi. I shall like to repeat my question to Mr. Matovina at this point, and I shall try to speak much slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yesterday, here you stated that a group of volunteers had left completely, all of them, a group of 600 men had left on buses, and there remained a group of 80 men who, with the locals or with this special platoon, as you called it, perpetrated the massacre. Well, if according to my information there was 600 volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party there, and if all the 600 of them left, the entire group, why would there remain a group of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party with a group of men from the White Eagles if they -- the others had all left? Isn't that a bit strange to you at this point?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you will allow me to shed some light on this, perhaps you didn't quite understand me yesterday. What I was saying was the majority of the volunteers from Serbia had left a day earlier, and of these 600 who were there, and we agree about that figure, of that 600, this group of 80 stayed on. Actually, in that situation, no one was able to count the heads, whether of this 600, 520 or 530 or 531 had left, but according to witness statements, most of them, the majority, had left prior to this event, and a group of 80 of the total number of volunteers who were there stayed on and participated in this crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay. Why, then, in 2002, did you not say the White Eagles and Seselj's men? Why didn't you associate in any place the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party or Seselj's men, as you called them, with this particular crime? Yesterday, you never associated the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party with the crime at Vocin.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that debate, nobody actually went so deeply into those -- in such a detailed way into these questions, but there is a list of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party and it was probably considered that on the basis of that list and the statements, it was quite clear who stayed there in the capacity of volunteers from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As you had lists of volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party from Serbia and you had victims and witnesses' statements, eyewitnesses to the massacre, perhaps you actually also had someone in custody who was accused of having participated in the crime. Were you able to identify at least a single one of the volunteers of the Radical Party and to say he's on the list of the volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, but we have this description that we discussed here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But not -- you did not identify a single perpetrator of the crime by name and can claim with certainty he was there and he is a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party; he was not a White Eagle, he was not from the Novi Sad volunteer unit, but a volunteer from the Serbian Radical Party or of the Serbian Radical Party. This you're not able to do; right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said these were volunteers from Serbia. In what capacity and on what basis, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But do you know that several volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were wounded, were captured in Masicka Sagovina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. That is not my province of interest, because throughout the war I was in Slatina. Masicka Sagovina is I don't know how many hundreds of kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, not hundreds of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, perhaps not, but it is not within the Osijek, Baranja, Virovitica, Podravska Slatina department. It is in another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you do not have a shred of evidence that at least a single volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party took part in the massacre of civilians in Vocin?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have proved that volunteers were there. You have proved that volunteers left. You have statements there the White Eagles did that, and only later, subsequently, you remember that there might have been a Seselj's man or two there as well?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I said. We use the term "members of the Serbian Radical Party." You now just said yourself "Seselj's men." How they were perceived in the eyes of the individual victims, that varied. If someone was a member of the Serbian Radical Party, and you being the leader of that party, I'm not quite sure, but perhaps the term "Seselj's men" is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It is formally not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... in questions and answers, because the interpreters cannot follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know what, I'm not disassociating myself from that. If these were volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party, at least I'm morally responsible for everything which they have done, and I'm not at all ashamed because other people called them "Seselj's men," or because somebody introduced himself, his own self, as a "Seselj's man," but the official designation was never "Seselj's men," it was always volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. But the people often did call them "Seselj's men." What I wish to clarify here are a few things. Given the fact that they were strictly instructed not to interfere with other groups of volunteers, not with Arkan's men, not with the White Eagles, nor with Draskovic's Serbian Guard and many other formations, units. Of course they could act in concert in combat occasionally, but there should have never been any organic interference or amalgamation of them, and this was the instruction they got on departure. So when you say that something was done together by the White Eagles and Seselj's men, that is absolutely unacceptable. Now, had you stated in your first statement "White Eagles and Seselj's men," I could hardly challenge it, because you are a police inspector, you were the chief of the crime investigation department, you were in charge of the investigation, and you did your best to diligently and conscientiously conducted, and you would have known exactly and identified the perpetrators of the crime. And you were younger and fresher, but -- you were younger and fresher when you exclusively referred to the White Eagles, and not a single reference is made there to Seselj's men, whereas six years after that, last night, you said also "Seselj's men." Was it my absence that actually influenced you to remember that Seselj's men were there, or did someone actually suggest to you that you should insert them as well?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no suggestion of that kind at all. What it was is that in that year, we used this designation to cover all volunteers from Serbia who are in the area of Vocin and beyond, farther afield, and I have already said that. So all the members of the different fractions that you are also referring to, yourself, and mind you, yesterday on the basis of the list of the units, both lists that we discussed yesterday, we went into detail in order to clarify how the event had actually transpired and who had taken part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now you have given us an even more incredible statement; namely, that you called all volunteers from Serbia "White Eagles." Nobody has stated that as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I think we need to clarify a mystery here. In 2002, when you made a statement, you mentioned the White Eagles. Apparently, you did not mention Seselj's men. You are a professional. For years, you've worked in the police force, carrying out investigation. In 2002, the indictment against Mr. Seselj was not made public. At the time, it did not exist, because Mr. Seselj was only indicted in 2003. In 2002, when you met with the investigators of the OTP, during the investigation on Vocin, was there formal confirmation of the fact that the perpetrators of the crime were the White Eagles and Seselj's men, why didn't you say so in 2002? When you carry out an investigation as you did, you should say who the perpetrators of the crime are and what their motivations are. So in 2002, on the motivation or the authors, you were already in a position to say they were Seselj's men and the White Eagles, and you didn't say so. "Seselj's men" came about much later. There's a mystery here. Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I used the term "the White Eagles," as I've already said, to refer to all volunteers from Serbia, I did so on the basis of witness statements. I looked into the case file prior to my arrival here, and some of the witnesses referred to Seselj's men, others to the White Eagles, the third to the Black Hand. It depended on the actual perception of the individual witnesses and the victims of the different -- members of the different units. The term which was used then, one of the terms, "White Eagles," was recorded in the minutes, and then it was used from that point on for all volunteers from Serbia who stayed in the territory of Vocin. Right now, in the Vocin case file, you can find witness statements featuring all these names that I have already described and which I read also coming here to this debate here, to this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying today in Vocin's trial. What trial are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the case file, Vocin, which was submitted to the state organs, the state prosecutorial office of Croatia. This case file was completed, including the on-site investigation findings, the autopsy findings, video footage, and the detailed description of the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I'd like to backtrack somewhat in your investigation. We know that people were killed in Vocin. Unfortunately, you were not able to get interviews from them, but did you get interviews from witnesses who might have been spared and were able to see the authors of the crimes? During your investigation, did you ever interview people who were there when the White Eagles or the White Eagles and Seselj's men perpetrated the crimes? Do you have witnesses who have seen, for instance, "On this day, I was there, I saw such-and-such an individual arrive there and do this or do that?" Did you hear that type of witness, because the difficulty we have here in this type of international trial, which should be totally exempt from any reproach, the problem we have here is that we do not have all the elements. We're hostages to the elements brought about by the OTP and by the Defence, so we don't have all the elements, because the Judges here are in no position to gather evidence. And because of that, we're penalized. That is why I'm asking you all these questions, because I have no evidence here allowing me to think that there were live witnesses who were interviewed. So did you hear any witnesses who were able to tell you what had happened in Vocin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Mr. President, that every particular detail is of special importance, and we did interview eyewitnesses who were in Vocin that night and who fled, and who actually were spared death. I would really like it if some of those witnesses wanted to take the stand here; not just one or two, but a number of them to testify here, and to also give the statements which they gave to the police during the crime investigation before this August tribunal, because it is on their statements that we actually based our findings in the crime investigation procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This investigation only finding out about, so obviously some witnesses made statements. And you explained to us that you discovered lists of members belonging to the so-called volunteer group, but your witnesses, did they say that the aggressors were people wearing military uniforms or weapons, but they weren't able to say they were Seselj's men, or the White Eagles, or X, Y and Z? Were they very accurate on the identity of the perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, some of the witnesses stated that the massacre had been committed by the most extremist local members of the special platoon of the White Eagles. The others said that it was with the Seselj men -- Seselj's men. Still others said it was the volunteers of the so-called Black Hand. And then some said that in late October, Mr. Seselj had visited his men in Vocin, and all these statements exist in the form of official notes and records, and they were the basis for the further forensic investigations, and it was in that way that we obtained the information we're referring to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are confirming that several witnesses indicated several possibilities; White Eagles, Seselj's men, the Black Hand, all sorts of possibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, you gave your statement to the Prosecution on the 11th of March, 2002, and then it was said that you would be called as a witness in the trial against Mr. Milosevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then you testified in the case against Mr. Milosevic on the 7th of October, 2002; in other words, six or seven months after you gave the statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Prosecution never told you that you were planned to be called as a witness in my trial; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I testified in the Milosevic case, I told them that I hoped that my appearance before the Tribunal would end there. I was told at that point that if ever they should need my assistance in a case relating to Vocin, that I would be called. And that's what, in fact, happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But no name -- my name, in fact, was not mentioned to you at the time, was it?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's a very important piece of information for me, and I want to corroborate that by the fact that according to what Carla Del Ponte said, it was in 2002 that the then-Minister Djindjic ordered that I be arrested and extradited. Therefore, there was this gap of six years during which you didn't have any contacts with the Tribunal, did you?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when was it for the first time that you learned that you would be a witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A month or two ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it was only a month or two months ago?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that it's been more than five years that you were kept in the records of the Prosecution as a potential witness before the Tribunal; were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The statement I gave -- or, rather, the testimony I gave in the earlier trial --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, let us not waste time. I need your direct answer. You said that it was a month and a half ago or two months ago that you first learned that you were supposed to testify in this trial. I'm telling you that the Prosecution put your name on a witness list more than five years ago. Therefore, all the while, you were in their list as a witness in my case without being aware of it. Now, when they approached you a month or two ago, how did they go about it?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a notice that I should testify about the crime that was committed in Vocin, as well as on all the other crimes that took place in a given timeline in the area of Slatina, all the way through to the Vocin event, where a massacre was committed and which marked the ending of the provisional occupation of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were informed of this in writing, were you not?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter. In writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Matovina, it is important. Tell me, how did they go about it? Did they place a phone call, did they send you a letter; how did they go about it? It's very important.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed about this over the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who called you?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was the Prosecution staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the call placed out of The Hague or Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both from The Hague and Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who called you from Zagreb, who was it?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lady, a staff member. I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it the office representing the ICTY in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. So a month or two months ago, you received this piece of information. What was the next contact that came about?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in touch with the staff of the ICTY and of the Prosecution, and I told them that I was going to repeat everything I stated in my earlier testimony, and that I would state the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And this is what we did, in fact, in the course of my yesterday's testimony, when we referred to the early days, the propaganda, the attack on the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're repeating your testimony here. Please, don't waste my time this way.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not wasting time. I said that I would stick to what I had stated earlier, and I was invited by the Prosecution to appear before the Tribunal, and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please. A month and a half ago, you were contacted over the phone, and between that and your yesterday's evidence is the period that I'm interested in. I'd like to know all the contact that you had between that first phone call and your yesterday's testimony, and you keep evading that.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not evading that. I went through the list and the case file and the statement again with the Prosecution staff because I wanted to make sure that all the data on which the criminal investigation and file is based is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may have been 10 or 15 days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And where did that take place?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As a police officer, you have to be more precise. I seem to come across as a better policeman than you are, and I haven't even come to the use of force in my investigation or in my examination. Can you tell me when and where was that in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICTY has its premises there. Therefore, it is of no importance now. Everybody knows what the address is. I don't know, personally, and I don't think it's important to tell you where it was that we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't think you can be the one to judge what's important.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm stating the facts, because the Trial Chamber finds facts relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: To let you know, I proofed the witness last week in Zagreb. It was a normal proofing like as the witness comes to The Hague and gets proofed here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor cannot answer instead of the witness, he cannot be testifying. I will not allow this. I think this is the -- an effrontery of the Prosecution. I don't want to engage in the examination in this way, because the Prosecutor is testifying instead of the witness. The witness said it was 10 or 15 days ago in Zagreb, and now the Prosecutor intervened and stated that it was a week ago in The Hague, and I've just caught the witness lying. What sort of an examination am I conducting here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question of the proofing, as far as I know, this takes place in The Hague, and I'm discovering now that this can take place elsewhere. The proofing session was held in Zagreb, this may be an important point. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness did not understand the point I was trying to make with my questions, and he kept saying that these matters were not important. He would want to teach the Trial Chamber about matters that are important. And then he went on to say that the proofing session was held in Zagreb. Now, when I tried to find out where it was, the address and so on and so forth, Mr. Mussemeyer sprang to his feet and stated that it was a week ago and that it was in The Hague. And I caught the witness lying, and this was quite an innocuous lie, in fact, but I made my point in showing that the witness is lying, and that's the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj wanted to establish something. Personally, I don't see the point of it, but maybe we will discover what it is a little later. Before coming here, you met with the OTP. As a rule, you arrive the day before or a few days before your testimony, and the OTP meets with the witness. In your case, this happened in Zagreb. Can you confirm that you met with the OTP in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true, that's what I said. Mr. Seselj misunderstood that, whether it was a couple of days earlier I was called and the Prosecutors of the ICTY were on other business in Zagreb, and I attended the -- a short proofing session. I believe that even Mr. Seselj understands that this is -- it doesn't pose a problem of any sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when did you meet the representatives of the OTP? Theoretically, we should have heard another witness today, so you are a replacement witness, because the witness who was due to testify has not come. So last week already, we knew that there was a likelihood that you would be coming to testify this week, and this is why you're here today. This is why it is important to understand at what point you met with the OTP in Zagreb. Was this a week ago, ten days ago, two weeks ago, three weeks ago; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know it was a Wednesday. I don't know whether it was the 5th, the 6th or the 7th. I'm not sure about the date. It may have been the 7th, and today we're, what -- well, it was eight to ten days ago. I didn't think it important as a piece of information. I am a criminal inspector, and I've taken part in so many investigations, but I didn't think this was important. I think it was on the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was on a Wednesday. At some point, did you lie when you answered some of the questions or did you always tell the truth about the contacts you had with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always spoke the truth. I always responded to any calls that came from the Prosecution. This was the sort of job I did. This is my day job, whenever I'm asked to produce reports or to give accounts of the events that took place. Yesterday, we spoke of the number of individuals who were able to give witness statements. Of course, I always responded to their invitations, and I believe my cooperation was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood correctly, when you testified in the Milosevic trial, the OTP told you at the time that you might have to come back to testify again. But at that time were you told that you would have to come to testify in Mr. Seselj's case or were you given no information whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seselj was not mentioned at the time. What I was told was that when and if there should be a case related to Vocin, "it is quite possible we would invite you again."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. When exactly did you learn that you would be coming to testify in Seselj's case? On Wednesday, the 7th of May, when did you learn this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, it was during my contacts one and a half or two months ago, when the Prosecution informed me that I was to be called as a witness in the Seselj case. Since I'd been following the case against Seselj, and since I was told at the end of my testimony in the Milosevic case that I might be called, once I was contacted, I knew that I would be a witness in the case, and I knew that what they told me at the end of my earlier testimony would, in fact, come true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just given us a piece of information. You said you followed Seselj's case. Why did you follow Seselj's case, and when did you start following Seselj's case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, being a criminal inspector, you know, once a policeman, always a policeman. I think you'll agree with me. I had been following all the proceedings before this Tribunal, and I also follow other proceedings before other courts, and I likewise followed the exchanges between Mr. Seselj and Judge Schomburg, if I'm correct about his name. I recall the Judge asking him not to be so harsh and to work in favour of his own interests. I found it all very interesting, and I always was interested in reading such information from the press or hearing broadcasts, and it was not just in the Seselj case but in all the others as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, did you feel the urge at that point to come before the Tribunal and to assist Judge Schomburg and help him from my attacks?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw the goodness in the Judge, who I believe disarmed you with his goodness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I have been disarmed by your goodness now here, and I have to examine you. And you, the Croats, have been enchanted with the German goodness for a thousand years, have you not?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, goodness comes from the mercy of God. I should suppose that you have that sort of goodness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Me, God forbid that I should have such goodness ever. But let us go back to our examination. You've had your proofing session with the Prosecution, and during that session, let's set aside the fact that you contacted the Croatian authorities, because you will not admit to that -- in the course of that session, Mr. Mussemeyer -- or Mr. Mussemeyer, I may have been mistaken in the name and perhaps the interpreter can help me, showed you the statement of yours from back in 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you read through the statement, both of you, there and then?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the statement through, although I still had it fresh in my memory, all of the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when you saw the portion of the statement toward the end, where you speak of the Vocin incident - that's the headline - you were able to see that your statement says that the massacre was committed by a paramilitary unit from Serbia, the White Eagles. Did it not occur to you at that time to tell Mr. Mussemeyer that it was not just the White Eagles, but also the Seselj's men who were there, that somebody had been mentioning during your investigation "Seselj's men" as well? Did you mention that?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. As I told you, I went through the Vocin case. There were some statements there also which were obtained after I stopped working on that case, and on the basis of that, I was able to see that various witnesses used various titles when referring to Serb volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, please answer my questions in a straightforward manner. You're a policeman. Just as you asked your suspects to give you straightforward answers and not to beat about the bush, I will do the same thing and ask the same thing from you. When you were having this proofing session, and looking at this portion of your statement with Mr. Mussemeyer, did you draw his attention to the fact that this portion should also include Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. This is the statement that I stand by, that I signed, and we merely wanted to see whether all of the details of the statement still stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, then, Mr. Matovina, you astounded Mr. Mussemeyer and myself when you added the "Seselj's men" to the "White Eagles." I saw Mr. Mussemeyer was astounded and taken aback about something, but I understand what. I did see him taken aback. Did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right. I said I was saying this on the basis of the knowledge I had from crime investigation. I was not up there, and I didn't count a single member of the White Eagles or the other units. I'm speaking about what the crime investigation showed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 2002, were you still a policeman?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 2002, you'd already seize ceased working on the police force?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So that means from 2002 to 2008, you were not able to gain any new knowledge from crime investigation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't, but it's in the files. I can look it up in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're testifying here now, and then we never see each other again. So the Prosecution doesn't have the time to bring you into court five times. It's got other false witnesses that are going to take the stand here. But, Mr. Matovina, what were you doing in 2002?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, don't say that they have other false witnesses. First of all, you know nothing about it, and this does make the witness sound suspicious. For the time being, he's answered all your questions. Witness, you are a specialist in investigation matters, so you know how important the questions are and how important the answers are. When the representatives of the OTP meet with you in Zagreb, you said, "They show me the statement and I read over it again," and then you say that at no point in time did Seselj's men -- were "Seselj's men" mentioned. It seems that this came to you as a surprise when he heard you talk about the White Eagles and Seselj's men. I assume that when he met you, unless he speaks B/C/S, there must have been an interpreter. Was there an interpreter there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an interpreter present, and I think that in that whole incident, everything was clear, as far as we were concerned, all those who were there. The concept of the White Eagles, as far as we were concerned -- well, I've explained it, I've explained what it means, and we just have to look at the statement. We saw the tape, the footage about the injury of those two citizens who were beaten up. We've already seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's take it one step at a time. On Wednesday, the 7th of May, you met a representative of the OTP, and you discussed with the OTP the content of your testimony today. And on that day, you did not mention Seselj's men, and you talk about Seselj's men when you came yesterday. How come, and how is it that during -- for all those years, Seselj's men were never mentioned and they now are mentioned out of the blue at the last minute? This is mentioned at the last minute because your memory no longer fails you or because you followed Seselj's case and you know that this is a key issue in this case, or is it that you feel that the words "White Eagles" was a generic term that encompassed Seselj's men, and at the time in 2002, when you mentioned the White Eagles, to you, in your mind, these included Seselj's men as well? So what is the reason? There could be several reasons. You understand my question, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely that, Mr. President. The concept of "White Eagles" implied all the volunteers from Serbia, and in the witnesses' perception of the matter and how the victims saw it and in coming here, I looked through the case, and I said I'd tell the truth, and I came across several official notes and reports and witness statements, and I'd like them to appear before this Tribunal. Some mention Seselj's men, others mention the White Eagles, others again speak of the Black Hand. Another set mentioned members of the Radical Party. So this name, "White Eagles," was found by witness statements, and it is through them that we arrived at this information. So that's all I'm saying. And when I looked at those official notes and statements, I'm conveying to you what they said, and I'd like at least a few of them to appear here before the Tribunal so you can see all three statements by these witnesses and how we recorded what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't doubt that your services could produce a thousand false witnesses, Mr. Matovina. That wouldn't surprise me at all. But tell me this: When you retired, you liked -- at least out of hobby, that you liked dwelling into police affairs, reading about them in the press, following various trials, legal proceedings and things like that, as a hobby?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a free country, and you can read the papers and watch television and follow what's happening; not only police investigations and events, but other events too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What else have you been doing since you retired?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all sorts of things. I did a bit of farming, and fruit tree growing, I was a deputy in the county assembly and in the district assembly for half a mandate, I was the deputy of the county head, the Virovitica County.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were quite active, politically, and well respected?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to an extent, that was the level. And as deputy of the county governor, you had quit a lot of public appearances. I found testimony to that. Well, from my own area of activities, social activities and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now during that period, did anybody file any criminal reports against you?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anybody did. I don't know that anybody did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Never?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody told me about it. This is the first I've hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know about the Croatian Social liberal Party; have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It's a police partner in the county assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean where you were the deputy?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the coalition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were an expression of the power of the coalition in which the Croatian Social Liberal Party took part; there was the Social Democratic Party and the Socialist National Party?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the SDAP and the HNS was the opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What other party was with this Croatian Social Liberal Party and the coalition?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Party of Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that Dzapic's party?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Before that, it was Paraga's party; right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Paraga was another faction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And to which of these parties do you belong?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I belonged and still belong to the Croatian Democratic Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So that's the third party in the coalition?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who is the president of the Croatian Democratic Union?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Ivo Sanader.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it's Tudjman's -- the person who inherited from Tudjman, right, the present prime minister?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what about the criminal report against you by the Social Liberal Party, Croatian Liberal Party? May we have it on the screen, and since it's not a secret document, may it be shown in public, in open session, please. Let's see what your former coalition party thinks, former and present.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've heard about Sinisa Kosutic, I assume.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's the former director --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Much has been said about coalitions of late. Witness, I don't know what document is about to be shown to you, but either you know that there is a criminal report, and you are under oath, or you don't know. You said you don't know. Can you confirm that you did not know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is the first time that I hear that a criminal report has been raised against me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You say you knew about Sinisa Kosutic. He was the manager of a company called Duhan from Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to this document, the director of Uskok in Zagreb, the organisation for crime and corruption prevention, raised a criminal report against 17 individuals suspected that from 1993 to 2002, through various legal -- illegal acts, deprived the company Duhan of many millions, and we see the specific facts there. In the second paragraph, it goes on to say -- or, rather, it describes what was done; illegal appropriation of four million-odd German marks at the time of the Belgrade Jugo bank in Slatina and so on, and then in paragraph 3, it says on the list of suspects we have former members of the board, Vinko Hmelik, Mato Dunkovic, Zlatomir Kramar, Ivan Bajt, and Ante Jimara. And Kosutic claims that through their work, they enabled these losses to be incurred in the Duhan company amounting to more than 90 million kunars. The crime report reached the Uskok organisation and actually was taken against Djuro Matovina, Zvonimir Kasumovic, those were the suspects, and they are suspected of enabling the former director, Zeljko Kolaric, to engage in business which deprived the Duhan company of many millions. Now, you know all these people there, you were a member of the supervising board of the Duhan company, and you say you don't know about this crime report?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I see this criminal report, and many times I had meetings with Sinisa Kosutic who for a time was a director of the company called Duhan when I was a member of the supervisory board, and he was replaced. Now, all these other men were members of the supervisory committee, and this is tendentious and false. None of these facts are true. Nobody ever contacted me, as far as this report is concerned, no one informed me about it, neither does any of this here stand, because the losses incurred by the company, as alleged here, they cover a number of years from the war onwards, and they were the result of other circumstances and not anything that Mr. Kostic stipulates here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, whether this is correct or not, I'm really not interested in any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Mr. Seselj. This criminal report that we've just seen, well, seemingly this was made public, since this report says: "HSLS." So this was made public. This criminal report, from what I understand, it's closely connected to a financial scandal. I don't see how you are involved in this, but we are not trying this particular case, rest assured. But what do you have to say about this document? The accused in these proceedings is entitled to test the credibility of the witness, so while doing so, coming up with a document like this enables him or us to have an understanding of your character and to check what you are saying. What do you have to say about this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I would like to know, first and foremost, Witness, because I don't understand this in B/C/S, I would like to know whether we're dealing here with a copy of a criminal report that's been filed. I don't understand if this is a mere comment made about a criminal report that's been filed or complaint. Could you specify this for me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see here it says: "A branch of the Liberal Party of Slatina." That does no longer exist anymore. It's not the Croatian Social Liberal Party which is in coalition in the county assembly. This Liberal Party no longer exists. At one time, the person who signed it, the self-appointed president, he's not the president anymore, nor is he active in any way anymore. So this isn't a criminal report. It's a pamphlet, that's all it is. And here it says: "The 24th of May," but I don't see what year. I don't see what year that was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Last year, Mr. Matovina.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see that. It says: "The 24th of May," up at the top, but no year. We can't see any year there. It says: "The 24th of May." "Vecernji List" is the paper. So I'd like to see exactly what year this was written in. It was published, as you can see, on the internet, on a website, and I don't know that this report exists in any of the official organs or offices of the prosecutor, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there an affair over this firm, the company called Duhan?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a company -- well, the situation was put to rights there, and I said that due to a number of circumstances, the prices on the world market and market trends generally, the company did suffer losses, but the situation was resolved. I have nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you a member of the supervisory board of the company?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we replaced three or four managing directors during that time, precisely for the reason that they didn't work to consolidate the firm and to deal with the difficulties the firm was going through, and that your intimations are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm not making any intimations. I just searched everything on the internet everything with respect to Djuro Matovina, and I received information what you did as the deputy prefect, what statements you made to the press and so on and so forth. And I set aside this criminal report against you, this of course is just information about the criminal report that was filed. It is an interpretation, in fact, of the criminal report. Whereas Mr. Matovina says that he doesn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you will agree that anything can be found on the internet, even accusations or libel, but not true criminal reports or proceedings started before a court. So I believe that this document, personally, is not reliable at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... asked to slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... which seems to be drafted by Dragutin Santosi. Your name appears in the middle of the document, and then, strangely enough, your name appears in bold type, as if it was meant on purpose for somebody to spot your name. And you're part of the board of directors of the Duhan company. Are you someone so eminent in this company that your name should be highlighted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not at all eminent. I can see that it was written by a general who is called Dragutin Santosi. It is published by Sinisa Kosutic and written by Santosi. I don't when he wrote it on the basis of what, I didn't see the date of the filing of the complaint. Well, you can see that it refers to 1993 to 2002 as the period in question. I really don't know. Nobody ever informed me of this, nor got in touch with me in connection with this. And this gentleman who wrote this, well, I suppose someone will call me one day and I will have a chance to say something on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know the person who signed this?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know Dragutin Santosi, and I find it very strange that he didn't inform me of writing this, it is very strange, because I do know him, and we are good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You will have something to discuss with him when you go back to Slatina.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, so we have established that it was for the first time last night that you referred to Seselj's men --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I'm sorry to interrupt, but we've now come to a good time for a break, and we'll take a break for 20 minutes. We'll resume in 20 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll resume our hearing. Mr. Seselj, you still have an hour and 18 minutes. This is what the Registrar told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, I'm going to ask you easier questions now than the ones which I put to you before, so you will be able to have a bit of a respite.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me -- I have completed it, I wrapped it up successfully, the previous portion of my questions. You worked in the police force for 30 years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did you stop working, what year was it?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of June, 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the year. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: When did the witness stop working? The interpreter did not catch from you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The year 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And if the witness and the accused would kindly not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And I'm also asked by the interpreters to ask you once again not to overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You remember that about the time you started working for the police, he was the chief of the municipality TO staff; right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure what positions he held. I know that he was in the state administration. I'm not quite sure what positions he held. I was not close to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But do you remember when he barged into the police station in Podravska Slatina with a pistol?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You do not remember? You were not in the station?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that even.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that an indictment had been filed against him before the County Court in Slatina -- in Bjelovar, sorry, for the Vocin crime?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's one of the people that I talked about in the list -- one of the people on the list of the Papuk Detachment. How the process ended before court, the investigation, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please be brief.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they were accused. I don't know in what stage the trial is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that he was the commander of the so-called Reconnaissance Platoon of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his role was in the list which we considered in some detail yesterday, and you can exactly see what functions he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that the position, commander or the leader of the Reconnaissance Platoon?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly on what list he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We didn't see his position in the list yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is on the list in the Cyrillic script, that list. He is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But here in the courtroom, he actually portrayed himself as a man who provided humanitarian assistance, accommodation for refugees. Do you know that he was a humanitarian worker or a combatant?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after the war that he worked with the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We're not interested in what he did after the war.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he provided aid to refugees during the period when this area was under temporary occupation, and this occupation lasted for four months, when the organs of the Croatian government did not function there, so we did not have full insight into who was doing what. So I don't know whether he did it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But he was accused for Vocin and for Cetekovac?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was accused for Cetekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And for Vocin, he was?
