utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is in the criminal complaint in connection with Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But do you know that the direct intervention of the US Embassy, Zagreb, the proceedings against him were suspended, were dropped?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During the war and before the war, actually, you were the first operative officer of the Slatina SUP; right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was one of the assistants of the commander of the police station, as I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay. And at that time when you were high police official in Podravska Slatina, murder of Serbian civilians started occurring; right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, there were several murders that took place in war circumstances and which were investigated as a crime, and criminal complaints were filed against unknown perpetrators. And we continued to collect information. Some of the perpetrators were identified and put on trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember the killing of Savo Smajlic, who was burned in his house?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This happened in Gornji Miholjac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were his killers identified, detected?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember the murder of the old lady whose surname is Potacek [phoen]? I could not learn the name, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was also done by unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember Milutin Gunjevic, a private entrepreneur?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: His killer were not found, either?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This happened before the war, by unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but in Podravska Slatina, a territory under Croatian control, and the victims were Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember the murder of an old lady whose surname is Katic? Unfortunately -- I could find her name, but I would have to consult my papers.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what about Zivko Bukarica, his killing? He was from Aleksandrovac.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the killing of Mile Komatetic [phoen] from Cojlug?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you remember that Gojko Olaca [phoen] had his throat slit at the very beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, Mr. Seselj is probably going to draw up a list of victims, and of course as I already said, unfortunately we Judges don't have all the evidence, and sometimes we have to go fishing for information. Yesterday, you told us that at some point in time at the police station, a thousand people came, and you described the whole situation very well. Now, I'm wondering whether the situation itself wasn't the consequence of a previous situation, all the crimes that are being listed by Mr. Seselj took place before the famous riot with the thousand people who came.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These crimes took place after the demonstrations and the attack on the police station in war circumstances that obtained in Slatina. This Papuk platoon that we -- or rather detachment that we discussed yesterday attacked Slatina with over 400 artillery attacks. We had over 10.000 refugees. The people who had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm interested in for the time being is these victims were Serbs, whose list has been provided, you just said that those were victims after the demonstration. So in a city or in a village, there are always people who are killed for reasons which have to do with delinquency because they are being robbed or pick pocketed or whatever. But those Serbs who were killed, why were they killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that they were Serbs. As I've already said this happened in war circumstances when we also have another massacre. These killings occurred in 1991, when we also had another massacre, the killing of Croatian soldiers, the arrival of refugees, the shelling of Slatina. So it was a general -- a wholesale nightmare against this setting these individual murders took place by unknown perpetrators as revenge, and these Serbs were the victims of individuals. And we acted in prevention, to prevent such things from happening, and we processed every individual case and investigated the individual crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those isolated individuals, were any of them arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some were identified and processed. Some are still unknown to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And those who were recognised as being the authors and then arrested, what argument did they present to justify their action? What did they say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did what they did as a consequence of hate. There was one instance which the gentleman perhaps didn't mention here, enumerated a lot of them, which was motivated by property motives. Some people killed a man, ransacked his house, looked for money and valuables, so this kind of thing that happens in war. Criminals of all ilk try to do their thing, as it were, so perhaps some were killed out of hate, because they were Serbs, but also there were property-motivated criminal offences because the perpetrators thereof just wanted to get some valuables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us assume that in a period of trouble, some authors of petty crime come here to rob or loot. Okay. But whether they're Serbs, Croats, Muslims, it's not an issue; they attack anybody. But did you feel that during the period the specific target was Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course, and with the police officers we had at the police station, namely, 70, we tried to prevent further crimes. The police was the only armed force, because it was only in the month of October of 1991 that the Croatian Army was formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990-1991, you were in the state called "Yugoslavia." The army in charge in the period of trouble was the JNA. If there was an insurgency of that type with individuals attacking Serbs or possibly Croats, and should the police not be in a position to protect the general population, would the police authorities ask for the help of the JNA to bring back order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, the army did not want to have any sort of cooperation with the police. The process of the division started. The first multi-party parliament was constituted. The JNA was proclaimed to be an enemy. I spoke about this in response to Her Honour's question. The army was using its weapons to arm local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that yesterday, that the army distributed weapons, but maybe if the army could not restore order, it felt that it should provide weapons to those in danger. Couldn't that be a reason for the weapons distribution? What's your opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that's the case, since the army appropriated all the weaponry that previously belonged to the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and those weapons were distributed among able-bodied men out of whose ranks the rebel units were formed. The murders referred to by Mr. Seselj had only civilians as their victims. These were not people who joined the ranks of army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, the JNA was supposed to be neutral or unbiased vis a vis Serbs or Croats, since it was the Army for Yugoslavia, but you said they distributed weapons to Serbs, not to Croats. In other words, the army was biased towards one of the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Yesterday, we referred to the 40-lorry convoy, about the distribution of automatic weapons and the training of men in the Papuk area. They simply intervened and saw an enemy in the Croatian police, which came to be true later on with the attack on the police station, the aim of which was to destroy that feature. The intention was for Slatina not to have any sort of police force and for chaos to set in. I said that we had tens of thousands of refugees passing through the area. We had air raids on several occasions which were, in fact, called for by the rebel forces. Besides that, we had artillery attacks, shells landing on both Croat and Serb homes, and because of the danger of further artillery attacks, there was a blackout in the town of Slatina. In such circumstances of war, many things happened, and we tried to maintain law and order as far as was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. You said that there was an artillery attack. You're saying the attack was on -- or landed on Croat and Serb homes. Were shells landing on any type of homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indiscriminate shells landed on the general area of the town, the industrial area, residential areas, whereas the aircraft also targeted various vital institutions, sport institutions, the police institution. But that was at the time when the Croatians took control, and it was the rebel forces from Papuk who did that. The Papuk area was under occupation for four months. There was a line of separation, and in that area the Croatian authority did not have control. So it was out of the area where the rebel forces were present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So the insurgency forces in Papuk were shooting or shelling the town indiscriminately. They were also shelling Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They shelled the general area of the town. In that period, most of the Serb inhabitants left, and many of them tried to evacuate their families to Serbia or to the occupied territory, out of harm's way, because they believed that the Podravska main highway would soon be severed and that the entire area would soon be captured. However, it was Pakrac that proved to be a bone of -- an obstacle, and this prevented them from cutting off the entire area of Slavonia, from cutting it off from the rest of the country, but they failed in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had all the Serbs left Slatina or had some remained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not all of them left. Many of them stayed there throughout the war, and many of them returned. Members of -- or, rather, the family members of those who were members of various units had been evacuated, because they knew of the lurking danger coming out of the presence of the rebel forces up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand correctly, the Serbs who had remained in their houses for whatever reasons were also shelled, just as their Croat neighbours who were shelled as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The town was shelled indiscriminately in order to create a psychosis of fear. And if you allow me to finish, in the morning hours, during the rush hour, when people went to work, or at night, at 2.00, and all this in order to create a psychosis of fear. The schools were closed for most of the school year. They only opened when the danger ceased, and that was in January. Those were war conditions. It was a nightmare, the backdrop against which all of this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To your knowledge, were Serbs shot or wounded by shots from Papuk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there were wounded. I'm not sure about the dead. Whenever the shelling started, and one already knew roughly the time when it would start, people knew where to seek shelter, although when the shelling started, it would start in broad daylight and it instilled fear. There were over 400 artillery attacks against Slatina with very heavy artillery weaponry, and I'm referring to Slatina and the general area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, these artillery positions at Papuk, how far away from Podravska Slatina were they, the artillery positions you claim -- from where you claim the attacks came?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was in the area of Lipovac, so six kilometres away, is Koralija, and then Bokan was another position some 300 kilometres away as the crow flies. They used the multi-barrelled rocket-launchers and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which sort of unit was that which had long-range artillery weapons that could reach the town?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the Papuk Detachment that had been armed by the JNA as it was leaving the area. Part of the heavy weaponry was found by us abandoned; cannons, mortars, even tanks, all of them were abandoned and then later on taken by the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many cannons -- how many guns did the Papuk Detachment have?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. It was the army who found the mortars, cannons, and the two tanks. One of the tanks had even been captured earlier. I didn't have that sort of information. The army did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So roughly there were two tanks, a lot of them were of the old make, D-55s, were they not, and perhaps a couple of cannons as well; is it not the case?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many cannons there were. The attacks were carried out by heavy mortars, 120-millimetre mortars, very destructive rounds. The positions were some two kilometres above Slatina, just opposite the line of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 400 artillery attacks, 400 cannon attacks, and not a single casualty. Isn't that a bit ridiculous?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were casualties. There were people killed and people wounded and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let us speak in more precise terms, shall we not. You were a police officer of many a standing in Podravska Slatina. Then after the war, for a while you were deputy -- what's it called? You were -- can you help me there?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy of the Virovitica Zupanija county Prefect, and that was just for a half term of office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So then you should know how many Croats were killed in the Slatina area in all during the war?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to speak from my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And I'm also referring to the Papuk area.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the Western Slavonia was not within my competence, and you know the area that you're referring to, the area that you're referring to, the area of Slatina is part of Western Slavonia, and I can't give you the number of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There is information about the numbers of Croats killed in the war in general; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So then you should know, being a local of the area, how many people were killed in Western Slavonia, how many police officers, how many soldiers, how many civilians?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't want to make a mistake, to be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, right. Can you then tell me how many civilian Croats were killed in total? There were 73 in Vocin, 24 in Cetekovac. When we sum that all up, what is the figure we arrive at?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were many more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I know, but you tell me.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 120 members of the army were killed, 24 policemen. There were civilians killed. Had I known you would put this question to me and that this would be the subject of my testimony, I would have obtained the accurate data. However, on the basis of the information we have, 24 Cetekovac, and then Vocin, 22 policemen, such-and-such a number of civilians. Well, there were many victims. Even one victim is one too many.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I agree with you that one victim is one too many, but the rough numbers are also important in order for us to see the scale of the war conflict and the scale of the killing of civilians. That would be a relevant piece of information. You mentioned 120 soldiers. Well, that's roughly the figure I have. 24 to 25 policemen. We could take that there were twice as many civilians. Could there have been twice as many?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If there were 150 soldiers and policemen killed in all, how many civilians would you add to that? And I'm referring to the entire period of the war.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I said would be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let us give an estimation. Would that be 200?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't want to speculate. I don't want to make any estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I can tell you that I know how many Serbs were killed. Can a document be shown to the witness, please, and I believe it was sent to both the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. You heard of the Serbian information centre called Veritas, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you knew it's led by Mr. Strbac, do you not?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that he's got very close cooperation and intense cooperation with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to the data he has, and that's from the 13th of May, 2008, that's the sort of information that the Prosecution would have, but for probably well-known reasons they wouldn't disclose them to me, so I had to contact Mr. Sabac myself. This is a list of all the Serbs killed in the area of Western Slavonia, those killed and who went missing. The list, and if you look at the last page, covers 1.086 individuals, and I made my calculations. We have the last name, first name, father's name, place and date of birth, municipality, date of when they went missing, municipality where they lived at the time when they went missing, a member, then they say whether they are civilians and so on and so forth, and the status, whether they went missing or were killed or were buried, and then the gender. We've got 502 Serb civilians listed here as those who were killed or went missing, and 584 soldiers and policemen killed. And this is much more than the sum total of the Croat victims. Now, you'll say that every victim is equally bad, but the figures do tell of the side which committed more atrocities. If we have 584 soldiers and policemen killed on the Serb side and 150 soldiers and policemen killed on the Croat side, then you can see the scale of the -- of deaths on the Serb side. And we have 502 civilians killed on the Serb side, and the Croats have not as yet opened the mass graves in Croatia. And you know that from Grubisno Polje and beyond, there were not -- there weren't any armed activities at all and we know how many people were killed nevertheless. What do you have to say to that, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You yourself stated that this refers to Western Slavonia, which is not the area we operate out of Virovitica and Slatina. In Slatina, where I was present, we had nothing to do with that area. You're drawing a comparison between the victims among civilians, soldiers and policemen on the -- of the Virovitica-Slatina area. You're talking about the towns, themselves, not even about the area of the county, and you are comparing those figures with the figures on the Serb side for the entire Western Slavonia, where the situation in the general area was different. We had the highway that was blocked, and without the Croatian Army carrying out Operation Flash, the area could not have been reached at all. I cannot comment upon these figures that you present me with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you're not aware of how many Serbs were killed or wounded during the Croatian Operation Flash, do you?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How come?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't even know how many civilians or soldiers were killed on the Croat side there, either. I don't know any of the figures relating to that. Why should we speak of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, let's move on. Do you know who Milan Vukovic was?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Savo Mackovic?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nikola Cevizovic, Milovan Ostojic, Vlajko Tomasevic?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are these names familiar?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But when you testified in the Milosevic trial, you said over there that you didn't know Milan Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of him, but I was never with him personally. I never heard any comments. I heard he was a judge in Pozega-Orahovac, and that he had an office and so on, but I never had any contact with him, nor did I ever talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But in the Milosevic trial, you said that you didn't know of him at all?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know him. I don't remember the detail. As for Vukovic, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, it's a good thing here, in 2002, you didn't know about Seselj's men, and now they've just come to mind. In the Milosevic trial, you hadn't heard of Milan Vukovic at all, and now suddenly you know him. So there's this natural process whereby your memory is improving little by little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait for the person who has put the question to end the question before you answer. Otherwise, you will be overlapping. Please answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm now going to give you some information about Milan Vukovic, and you can confirm or deny them. Milan Vukovic was a judge in Orahovac. He was the president of the District Court in Slavonska Pozega, and after that he worked as a lawyer. He had legal offices opposite the police station in Podravska Slatina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Several months before the war broke out, with some other Serbs, he was arrested by civilians, armed civilians, or rather para-policemen, armed civilians who acted as policemen. Did you hear of that case?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was brought in, and these other people that I read out, and you said you knew them, too. Anyway, they were escorted to the SUP yard of Podravska Slatina, and then Vukovic was taken into one of the offices, "the office of Djuro Matovina," it says. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He wasn't brought to your office?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I knew you'd deny that. Anyway, the first operative in the police station, where there was a certain man called Rostas? Do you know this man, Rostas? He was a teacher, and he's now the head master of the primary school in Podravska Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of the Croatian national guards school in Slatina, and he was indeed a teacher and the headmaster of a school. But he was never in the police station during the war, and to the best of my knowledge I never saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When these people are brought into your office, you were passive in your conduct, and Rostas had the main say?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. They were never brought into my office, never. I don't know Vukovic personally. I know Maskovic and the others, the names are familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please stop. The Prosecutor is on his feet, and I don't know why but he is about to tell us why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have a short remark. It would be helpful if Mr. Seselj could tell us where the witness in the Milosevic trial said that he did not know Milan Vukovic. I quickly checked in his transcript of the Vukovic -- the Milosevic trial, and I see on page 11068 to the question of Mr. Milosevic: "All right, let's go and engage in a general debate. Tell me, do you know a prominent citizen of Slatina a Serb, a lawyer by profession, Milan Vukovic?" The answer is of Mr. Matovina: "I don't know the man personally. I believe he's from Orahovica, if I pronounce it correctly, but I've never had any personal contact with him. I don't know where he is nowadays." So he did not deny completely that he did not know him at that time. This is only what I could find on a quick search. Maybe Mr. Seselj has a better source, but it would be helpful if he could tell us before he is quoting these things. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, after the questions are put, we understand that Milan Vukovic was a judge, he was a lawyer, and it seems that his house was on the other side of the police station. This is what we have learnt. And you said in the Milosevic trial that you didn't know him personally, you didn't know him at all. You had seen him by the by. Is that all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know him personally. He opened his offices just before the war and I never had any contacts with him, and I am grateful to the Prosecutor for helping me out and telling me exactly what I said in the Milosevic trial. And, actually, what I said then is exactly what I said here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where the premises of Elektroslavonija are located in Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, they are always in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what was there during the war and the conflicts?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was a torture house for Serbs over there, and you say "nothing." That's not true, sir. In your presence, Rostas decided and stated that Milan Vukovic and the other Serbs should be taken to the premises of the Elektroslavonija company. They were seriously beaten up there and afterwards returned to the yard of the SUP of Podravska Slatina where the torture continued. You personally, Mr. Matovina, observed all this and watched Milan Vukovic be tortured by having cigarette butts extinguished on his back; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Matovina. The accused seems to be incriminating you. According to our Rules, you do not have to answer. If the Trial Chamber decides that you should answer the question, then the Trial Chamber can grant you immunity for these facts. I must inform you of this possibility, since the cross-examination is charging you. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned the demonstrations in front of the police station, and in your statement you mentioned Rade Gajic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who was Rade Gajic?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the municipality at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was his role in that -- at that meeting or rally?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had been to the chief of the police station for talks, Mr. Kresimir Libl, together with Milan Karadzic and Ilija Sasic. But with your permission, Your Honours, may I be allowed to answer the question a moment ago linked to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You can do that, but outside my time. If the Judge gives you some extra time which isn't deducted from my time, I have nothing against that. But if it takes up my time, then just answer what I am asking you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you wanted to answer Mr. Seselj's question or not? I haven't quite understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, the question about the fact that four people were allegedly tortured and that I observed that, and that Mr. Rostas was there. I was never -- I never attended that event, nor do I know about any event like that. So thank you for giving me the opportunity of responding, and I am responding before the whole world and in front of the cameras here and state that that is a lie. It is tendentious -- tendentiously presented here to discredit me. My conscience is not burdened by anything, and that is the greatest thing I own and my greatest capital that I can say, my greatest property during the war. Mr. Seselj, you don't know me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't know you, and I have no intention of getting to know you, Mr. Matovina. You're a Prosecution witness, and I came across some data which go towards discrediting you in a serious fashion. But otherwise, I'm very doubtful that my time is calculated the same as the Prosecution time, because I find something strange in those calculations, so please don't deduct this from my time. You said that the motive of the demonstrators in front of the police station that their aim was to take control of the police station?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, just a minute. About the fact that you thought you did not have the same time allotted to you as has been allotted to the Prosecution, the time is being checked by the Registrar. It's she who tells us how much time you have had. And according to what she tells me, I inform you. I have nothing to do with that. At this point in time, I cannot tell you how much time you have left. It's Madam Registrar who will tell us. This is what I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Seselj used one hour and three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that the main object of the demonstrators in front of the police station was to take control of that same police station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, those 1.000 demonstrators, of which many had arms, had they wanted to take control of the police station, they could have done so at any point in time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that is not right. The demonstrators, who were armed and who had imbued alcohol, and who were doing some shooting, and turned over a car and injured someone, well, anyway, the term yesterday was very well used, the term that was used yesterday. Anyway, when they saw the resolve of the policemen to defend the police station and when they saw that they would come up against resistance and that this could spark a war, they gave up on the idea. Of course, after talking to the chief of the police station, chief of police, Mr. Kresimir Libl, when the leaders of the SDS came out, they appealed to the people gathered there to disperse, because they had been given assurance that the weapons of the reserve police force would not be displaced from the police station. So that was the reason, allegedly, why they intended to attack the police station, whereas the real reasons were others; to establish control over the police station, and this was already seen previously in Pakrac, in Orahovac and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's leave that alone. You weren't over there so don't testify about things you don't know about.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they are facts, they are things that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now you're provided us with the right answer, and that is that the rumour went through Podravska Slatina, that the Croatian authorities were preparing to take weapons away from the police station, as indeed had happened in many other places, where the majority were the Serb population, and all the demands by the mass of Serbs that had been collected there concerned the weapons from the police station that they thought would be taken away?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need to take any weapons out of the police station. Why would it, because it was necessary for the reserve police force. I don't know where the logic there was, that anybody should take the weapons away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the rumour was that the Croatian authorities wanted to take away the weapons as they had done in many municipalities populated by Serbs. Rade Gajic, who was a Serb and president of the municipality, entered among this mass of people to calm them down?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and speak one at a time. It is impossible to translate at this high speed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We discussed their appeal yesterday on the masses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please go more slowly. The interpreters have difficulty, find it difficult to keep up the pace.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, you described the case of Mato Mesaros in quite false terms. 1.000 people gathered in front of the police station, and Mato Mesaros was trying to make his way through that mass in a car; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he managed to make his way through this crowd?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did, but he ended up badly. He was driving his wife, who was very ill. That's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's leave that to one side, whether he was driving his wife. I don't know about that. But, anyway, he managed to drive through this mass of 1.000 people, although the police from all sides stopped the traffic once this crowd had gathered there; is that correct? Did the police indeed stop traffic in that street?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were not many policemen, we didn't have many policemen, and we found it hard to collect even that number of policemen to defend the police station, let alone deal with traffic, because there was the danger of the police station being taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nobody actually wanted to take control of this police station, did they? Now, Mato Mesaros drives through this crowd at low speed. He manages to pass through the crowd; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he manages to do that, he succeeds in driving through the crowd and reach the medical centre at Podravska Slatina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when he managed to reach his destination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, both Mr. Seselj and the witness, you have not understood that after your question and your answer, there is a translation. Therefore, you need to make a pause. You're not -- you're talking to each other. You're not talking to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When he finished what he was doing in the medical centre, whether he was taking his wife or whatever, it's immaterial, he drove his wife to the medical centre and left her there, he once again drove back through the masses; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, why did he have to pass through the crowd again when he was no longer in a hurry?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He considered that on his way back, the crowd had dispersed and that he would be able to get through, because there was no -- he didn't choose another route. This was the shortest route, and it was the main street, anyway, the main street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, think of this, Mr. Matovina: Can you imagine that in Zagreb, you have 1.000 people demonstrating somewhere in Zagreb, and then someone comes there and intentionally drives a car through the crowd, the mass of people there are angry. There's a lot of shoving and pushing, somebody is injured. And when this is all over, you have the same person coming back and driving through the crowd again, and in fact he injured ten people driving through the crowd. First of all, he had two alternative routes, he didn't have to pass through the crowd again at all; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had more than two alternative routes. There were more alternative routes that he could have taken. But why would he, because this was the main road, and there was no reason for the main road to be blocked off, and that there were demonstrations and unrest going on on that main road, and from there an attack should be launched on the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First of all, there was no attack on the police station, and it wasn't up to Mato Mesaros, that was the second point, whether the demonstrations were legal or illegal. When he saw a mass of people there, he should not have driven past the crowd. Imagine demonstrations in France or Denmark or anything, and then suddenly somebody decides to drive through the mass of people. Now how would the mass have reacted? Mato Mesaros could have taken the northern route and bypassed Brace Radica Street or, rather, the people gathered in front of the police station, taking the market route and Strossmayer Street. He could have avoided the mass, avoided the crowd.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that is indeed a bypass, but it was his choice why he decided to go through the crowd. He went legally through the main road. There was no need to shut off the traffic, that unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is lawful, in your law in Croatia, when a drive sees a pedestrian on the street, he has to stop the car, isn't that right, even if the pedestrian is outside the pedestrian crossing; isn't that what the law says?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is the principle of solidarity and mutuality in laws governing traffic, and you have to give up on your right-of-way if you run the risk of harming someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So this driver sees thousands of people, and he's thinking are they there legally or illegally, and having reached the conclusion that it's illegal, he just hits the masses; is that right? So which mass of people would it be that would not lynch him? Do you think that in Zagreb, if there was a trade union rally and if a driver behaved that way, that he wouldn't be beaten up by the crowd?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. We can only speculate and assume what could happen or not. But that was his choice, he decided to go that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see, his choice. So because of that choice, he was beaten up. He could have taken the southern route as well from Laze Tihomirovic Street further on and then Milan Klein Street, he could have taken that route, and then everything would have been fine; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's right, but I can see that you know the streets very well. It's almost like you're a local of Slatina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I might decide to live in Slatina, once Slatina is liberated from Croatia occupation and when Serb authority is established there as well, I might well choose Slatina to live there. I'm not going to stay here for 100 years serving time, I might be here 30 or 40 years, but I'll go and pass my final years and days in Slatina, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, no statement on the future is called for. What we want to know is what happened there at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Judge, you never intervened when this witness made inappropriate comments in relation to my questions, rather than answer them. What concern of his is it whether I know Slatina or not? He should answer my questions and not comment. Obviously, he's been instructed to just follow one line in his testimony, and that is the line of the "Seselj's men." Everything else is secondary, and those who instrumentalised him are not interested in anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the witness has carried out investigations. He must have realised that you mentioned the name of a street, which means that you know the city inside out. You might know it personally, or maybe some of your collaborators have shown you a map to show you how that individual who went through the mob could have chosen a different route. So I understood, personally, why the witness said that. Move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. If you understand it, I'm not at all surprised I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He had at least two routes available to him to bypass this crowd of people, did he not, and without anything happening to him; isn't that right, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said not only two but more routes, but the man opted for this main thoroughfare, and that was his choice. Why he made that choice, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And this time the crowd that was already angry because of his earlier penetration through the crowd, would not yield, and they took him out of the car -- stopped the car, took him out of the car, and started beating him; right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have spent a considerable time now discussing why this gentleman might have taken one or the other route. To me, this is mere speculation. You couldn't know why he took that route, nor could the witness. I suggest unless you have a very strong point to make here, that we move on to the next issue that you have to raise with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You do encourage this witness, and he can continue along this line that he's been instrumentalised to follow, and that doesn't surprise me at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, no, I disagree with what you've just said. My colleague, and rightly so, has just pointed out to you that you've spent a lot of time trying to find out why this individual chose to drive across the mob, with the consequences that entailed. We'll never know why he chose that route. It's pure speculation. And my colleague, and rightly so, said you should move on, unless you have a strong point to make, a decisive point to make. So we're not preventing you from presenting defences. You're saying we are encouraging the witness. No, we're not encouraging anyone. We are trying to find out what happened. Yes, like you, I wondered why this individual chose to drive through the angry mob. I wondered about that, too. Was it provocation on his part or was he, himself, extremely frantic because his wife was ill? It's all understandable reasons, and that type of incident occurred in many countries elsewhere, where people went through mobs and were abused or beaten up by the crowd. We've all heard about those. But if you're insisting on this, why are you insisting on it? Are you trying to show that that person was trying to provoke the crowd? We're willing to hear your assumptions, but so far we don't get your point. If you have a point of substance, why don't you ask the question to the witness so that we can understand what you're driving to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to ask a question, and you interrupted me. You never intervene in this way when the Prosecution asks the most senseless of questions and loses us the most time, but that is your criteria and I'm not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, you stated that when you saw that the crowd was beating Mesaros, that you ran up to them with another two policemen through the crowd in order to rescue him; is that true?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the crowd was so infuriated, so enraged, that you and another two policemen could, without any injury to yourselves, intervene, passing through a crowd of 1.000 people, and save this Mesaros, and then take him to a cafe, to a restaurant, and then wait for an ambulance to come by the back door and take him to an infirmary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the crowd was located along the street. It was not as if all the 1.000 people were in one single spot. Where there was this overturned car, when Mesaros was taken out, pulled out of it, this was in the direction of the motel of the Skajtering [phoen] establishment. And I intervened with these two policemen. I pulled the man out of the crowd and I removed him. I placed him in the Skajtering establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have said this, and this is quite true, I'm not denying it, I'm not challenging it. You're just wasting my time. But this crowd through which you passed to intervene knew you personally as one of the principal policemen in Slatina; is that true?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did know me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They knew that you were a Croat?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And instead of lynching you, too, here is an isolated Croatian and the chief policeman in Slatina, that not a single blow was delivered to you, but they enabled you to rescue Mr. Mesaros that the masses were rightly mad at; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct they didn't attack me. They didn't attack me and the two policemen, but they did attack Mesaros and hurt him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm going to explain to the Judges why I ask all these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're not letting the witness answer. You're basically speaking over him, and the interpreters get lost. I understand that you might be angry, but in legal matters, when you are dealing with a substantive issue, you need to remain calm so that the message gets across to those the information is intended for. Otherwise, you get angrier and angrier, and we lose track of the substance of the matter. You said you were going to explain to us what your point was going to be, so we're waiting for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, I have to explain that I'm absolutely not nervous. I'm using my capacity as an orator because this is a public hearing, and I'm here confronted with the Prosecutor, the witness and the Bench. I am demonstrating here that this witness is falsely portraying these demonstrations outside the police station, that it was an unruly crowd, that there were many drunken people, that they opened fire, that they intended to take the police station. All of a sudden, this very self-same witness, with another two policemen, passed through that infuriated crowd without any danger to himself and the other two policemen and rescues the man at which the mass was mad, without sustaining any injury, and that man who he rescued had hit 10 people passing through the crowd. And the fact that he mentioned that his intestines were on the asphalt, that is a lie, because he wouldn't have been able to save him. It is only true that that person was beaten and with justification. That is true. I would have done so, myself, had he tried to penetrate the crowd with an automobile. And I should also like to say that I'm not at all nervous, I'm not upset. I'm using my rhetoric faculties. I'm asking leading questions because I can do that. I don't have Mr. Riedlmayer here and I cannot follow his method. I have my own method, which is not at all in contravention of the Rules of Procedure nor those of cross-examination. So I fail to see why you're intervening. I've come to my point. This was a false portrayal of the demonstrations in Podravska Slatina, which I've just proven, and I've achieved what I strove to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, yesterday I myself wondered about the way in which you described the crowd. Just looking at the transcript, there's enough for that. And I wondered about the fact that even though you were a Croat, you went into the crowd without being injured, so this was also an observation that I made. And Mr. Seselj is pointing to that. You described what happened to the individual described above, and from your description the feeling was that he was almost killed on the spot by the riotous crowd. So in retrospect, with more calm, haven't you added details to the description of that crowd, and haven't you forgotten something that might have happened to you in the meantime, because you would have been an ideal target, given the state of that crowd? So have you added any elements, have you forgotten anything? What could you add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, distinguished Mr. President, I have told the truth, because I went through that event personally from the very point the gathering started, which is sometime around 1830, up to the culmination of this event at 2200 hours. So the atmosphere, the emotions and the highly-charged climate was not the same throughout the event as at the end, when there was shooting and the mass dispersed. Mr. Mesaros was badly hurt. He was operated on, and they saved his life, but with difficulty. His intestines were really hurt, and there is medical documentation in the hospital in which he was treated, which can still can be submitted to the Tribunal. Now, why didn't they do the same thing to me and these other two persons? They were policemen, and most of the people knew us. How we got through that without getting attacked, even though the catering establishment was later attacked with tiles that were thrown at it, which were there for the purpose of construction of a nearby building, some people actually went to the other side because they thought we had hidden him in the toilet. I still have the image vividly in my mind. It is etched in my mind. It was something that was extremely stressful and one of the most stressful moments from my career as a policeman. I've told you the truth, word for word. I have no reason to add or subtract anything from that. Now, why Mr. Mesaros went through the crowd, and certainly by passing through the crowd provoked the crowd to attack him, that is quite clear, but such brutality and what happened then, that is what I have described, and I have nothing to add to it or to take away from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you and the other two policemen, if I understand correctly, were armed, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj said earlier, among other things, at one point in time, that the car driven by Mesaros had injured people who were there. He said that very quickly, and it seems to me that I didn't hear about that yesterday. To your knowledge, even though this goes back a few years, when he got back into his car, he drove over some people, which could account for the violent reaction of the crowd, or is that an invention from Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people who were in front of the car were probably the ones who got injured, and they hit the roof of the car and the windows of the car. But whether they asked for medical assistance after that, I don't know, because there didn't arrive at the police any document to the effect that they had been hurt, they had been hurt when the car passed through them, because such documentation would have been part of the file on the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume there was an investigation after those incidents. Once Mesaros was operated on, he must have been heard about the incident. If people were injured in the crowd, I'm sure they were identified, unless it was general chaos and there was no investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were unable to identify the persons who directly attacked Mr. Mesaros, overturned his car and inflicted injuries, grave bodily injuries on him. Nobody was held accountable for that, because it was impossible to identify the perpetrators. It was night, there was a huge crowd assembled, so that we don't know to this day who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must thank you most sincerely, first of all, for the statement that I'm inventing things here. In all the hearings so far, witnesses have proven that I'm the only one who is inventing things in this courtroom, but it is a fact that the Prosecution witnesses are really faring very badly here, and that's on account of the flights of my imagination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let us go back to your statement. On the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, Mr. Seselj. You're not with the habit of thanking anyone, I'm really struck by your thanks here. When you said that people were injured, I felt that you must have evidence of that, and you could have said to the witness, "Well, from witnesses or my collaborators or myself know that person X was injured." That's a very solid argument. It's undeniable. But if you say people were injured, we don't know anything about that, and somebody might think that you're inventing something. That's all I said. So when you're making a statement, a judge, whoever that judge is, will feel, "Okay, but what is that statement based on? Is he inventing something? Is he adorning the truth? Is he speaking nonsense?" But if you're saying things and basing what you're saying on documents and evidence, then we'll feel that's a truthful statement, and it's a much more valid point. Otherwise, all we can do is assume things. This is why I asked the question again. I tried to check what you were saying. I asked the witness, "Was an investigation carried out," and he explained that the investigation did not lead to identifying the people. And you see that when you're saying something, I'm trying to check. I'm doing your work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, Judge, I believe we all agree on one point. I invented it, and the witness said that he did not exclude the possibility that there might have been injured people there. In other words, this figment of my imagination was something that the witness may have concurred with, and I, for one, may sometimes thank Their Honours, however strange that might seem. Now I'd like to go back to the statement Mr. Matovina gave back in 2002. There are some matters that the witness did not repeat in his examination-in-chief which I find very important and which will reveal to you which sort of witness is before you, if you'll allow me to go through the exercise I have planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, do you have the statement of yours? Can the Prosecution hand you the statement so we can go through it together, so that you're not compelled to give your answers off the top of your head?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's necessary. You have it. You can read it, and I'll answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to put you in an unequal position, me having your statement and reading it to you. I might perchance deliberately invent or make up some portions of your statement. I'd rather you have your statement, since you are a Prosecution witness. And while we're waiting -- or rather I should like the time during which we're waiting for the statement to be handed to the witness not be deducted from my examination time. I think it needs to be provided in B/C/S language to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have it on my screen, but I don't know if my computer is connected to any printer here. So I could print it. I don't know, if the printer's working, I hope it is the correct one. It's only the first page. We must wait.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to page 1 right away so that we don't waste time, and then we'll see to the other parts later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, you have this headline in the middle of the page which reads: "Situation before the conflict in the former Yugoslavia." And then in the first sentence of the first paragraph, you state: "According to the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences, there was an imaginary line of borders for a Greater Serbia that spread along the Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica axis, and this was an unfortunate coincidence for the Croatian people who live in this area." Is this what you stated for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever read the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So then why do you lie by saying that the Greater Serbia and the Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica line is mentioned there at all?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not lying. You mentioned these matters frequently in your speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I did, but not the Serbian Academy, and you're referring to the Serbian Academy here. Unfortunately for me, I was never even nominated as a cabinet member of the academy because I'm not good enough. I will be advocating a Greater Serbia for the rest of my life, and it is true that I was saying that the western border of Serbia runs along the Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica line, but why did you state here that this was according to the memorandum of the Serbian Academy? Why did you lie?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't lie, really. The memorandum writes about the efforts and the attempts to establish such a border.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're lying. You didn't read the memorandum, because nowhere in the memorandum does that say what you just said. And the Prosecution will have a copy of the memorandum of the Academy of Arts and Sciences. This is a ruddy lie.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe you have to read into the memorandum more closely and look into the general context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No. There is nothing of the sort envisaged in the memorandum. It merely speaks of the future of the Serbian people, and you lied when you said that you read it, and you lie when you say that this is what the memorandum contains.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, so you say, but I insist that you're lying and that you're on a mission here to lie. You go on to say the following: "In order to make the idea of a Great Serbia real, the areas in this line -- along this line were populated with rural Serbs from Bosnia." When was the memorandum of the Serbian Academy written; do you know?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated this because ever since World War II, that area had been populated by Serbs, wherever there was a home unoccupied. Therefore, in Vocin, in Bokan [phoen], Macute, Ceralije, Croats used to be the majority population. Along this imaginary line of Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica, that should have been the western border of a Greater Serbia, toward Vocin, the entire area, you know what sort of an ethnic makeup it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was: When was the memorandum of the Serbian Academy written?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date. You're asking me about details on matters that I only read in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'll tell you, it was written in 1987, and you're telling us that the rural Serb population from Bosnia populated this area in order for this imaginary line, and the truth is that it was mostly the Serbs who moved out of Vocin because they were in search of jobs. And where was it in Western Slavonia that you say it was?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gornji Gusani [phoen], Donje Gusani [phoen], Bijelijarac [phoen], Lisicine, the villages in the area toward Pakrac and Okucani.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is something you're making up. The Serbs and Croats from rural area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Dalmatia, Lika, were moved in order to populate the vacant homesteads previously populated by Germans who were moved out of the area with the end of World War II. This was merely a repopulation of the area?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're referring to the general area. However, the area which was the corridor of the imaginary border of Greater Serbia, this was an area which was deliberately populated by Serbs. And if you look at the ethnic makeup of the area, you'll know what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First of all, the Serbs had been living there since the 16th century. This was the border between Austria and Turkey. Serbs populated the area, and Croats had never lived there. In fact, the Croats you're referring to as living there are Serbs who were converted to Catholicism. There was never a colonization of Serbs after World War II, and it was in fact a rare occasion where Serbs from Bosnia moved over to the territory of Western Slavonia. It was a rare phenomenon. Now, as for the Serbs and Croats alike who were from Bosnia, Dalmatia and Lika, they were deliberately resettled to colonize the area that had previously been populated by Germans. The rest is something you invented.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is for the umpteenth time that I'm hearing that the Croats currently populating the area used to be Serbs, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that is the truth, and you spoke the Chekovian language too. Very well. Mr. Matovina, now you say that the populating of that area by Serbs was a strategic plan and that they would support the idea of a Greater Serbia. Was it Tito, then, who had plans for a Greater Serbia, and as part of that, he caused the Serbs to resettle there?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are history lessons you're giving us. What I'm -- what we have before us here are the statements I made and the conclusions I arrived at, and I believe I'm entitled to my own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, so you gave your opinion to the Prosecution and ultimately to the Trial Chamber, so these are opinions we have here. You should be a fact witness. So why did you state, then, that this was something that was contained in the memorandum of the Serbian Academy; is that an opinion of yours as well?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I'm not lying, and I told you that these are opinions and statements I made on the basis of facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So, Mr. Matovina, why are you placing the two Prosecutors in such an unpleasant situation, because both these Prosecutors read the memorandum of the Serbian Academy and they know that it does not contain what you say it does, so why are you doing this and why are you ruining their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. Witness, in your written statement, which I don't have before me, it seems that you said that the Serbs had sent for strategic reasons to go and occupy a number of villages and to go and work in those villages. Mr. Seselj is putting these questions to you and saying, "Well, these people, didn't they go there under Tito," which struck me, because if what you are saying is true, if the Serbs went there under Tito, well, then there was no plan with a view to establishing a Greater Serbia. So when you say these Serbs went there, what time, what date, what period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were large-scale migrations. Some of the areas I referred to had the majority Croatian population. In the past couple of years, some of the villages in the area of Slatina were populated by Serbs from the rural areas of Bosnia. I said that this process had been going back 50 years and that it was demonstrated in the armed rebellion that in these corridor areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One has to be very attentive here. You said that this process was a 50-year-long process, so these Serbian peasants who settled in these villages around Slatina did not come seemingly because Mr. Seselj told them to go there as part of his plan to establish a Greater Serbia; they went there decades ago already. So in your written statement, on reading that, one has the feeling that they have come at the request of the accused, so one has to be very accurate here. What did you want to say in your written statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. President, I have to intervene, and it will become quite clear to you why I keep saying that I am in confrontations with the Trial Chamber. Nowhere does Mr. Matovina, in his statement, speak of my ideas concerning the borders of a Greater Serbia. He ascribed my ideas to the memorandum of the Serbian Academy, and then he doesn't even know when it was written, even though it was written in 1987. And he presented everything that took place 40 or 50 years ago as a result, as a consequence of the memorandum. If you can stomach this, then it's up to you. I am not angry or upset. I'm merely trying to use rhetoric to brandish -- to pinpoint his lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you have to say to that? You heard what I said, you heard what Mr. Seselj said. In this memorandum of the Serbian Academy, which you are referring to and which you have read, according to you, when you tie that into what you have said in your written statement, one can conclude that this migration of Serbs towards that area is the consequence of this Greater Serbia plan. Thanks to you, we discover that these people arrive there 50 years ago. Does this mean that 50 years ago -- 50 years is 2008 minus 50 is 1950, and the memorandum was written in the 1980s. Does this mean that some Serbian peasants came to this area in Slatina and this had nothing to do with the Greater Serbia, with the memorandum, or Mr. Seselj's speeches, or something else, for that matter? This is what I'm trying to clarify, whatever Mr. Seselj might think. I'm trying to understand why these people went to that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us clarify this part of my statement. I didn't say anywhere that Mr. Seselj encouraged the migration of these people. I spoke of a strategic plan. It is not by coincidence that it was in the very corridor where the armed rebellion took place. Such migration processes had been taking part over 50 years, and that the ethnic makeup of the population there changed. It was in the corridor covering Vocin, Okucani and Pakrac, covering some 50 to 60 villages, that the population rebelled. The Croatian authorities had no control there. The police force was among the ranks of the rebels. Mr. Seselj, when speaking of a Greater Serbia, speaks of the borders, and the borders pass precisely across that area where the migration processes had taken place. I never stated anywhere that it was Mr. Seselj who had encouraged this or incited this, and we never discussed it before this moment. But I believed it necessary to indicate this issue at the outset of my statement in order to see clearly the further developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... plan, and this is what I remember, and my colleague remembers this, that Mr. Seselj is charged with a joint criminal enterprise, the purpose of which was to establish a Greater Serbia. This is one of the purposes of the criminal enterprise. And on looking at the way in which the events unfolded in Vocin, and you yourself have mentioned a strategic plan, one may well wonder whether the strategic plan is part of this Greater Serbia plan of the joint criminal enterprise and whether at that time, in the 1990s, Serbian peasants came to settle in the Slatina area. And you are telling us that you did not attribute this to Mr. Seselj, but as far as you are concerned, there is a strategic plan. So if there is a strategic plan, who, according to you, is the author of this strategic plan? Who was it initiated by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj said on several occasions today where it is, across which area, that the borders ought to pass, and he even said that he had plans of perhaps settling in Slatina one day, if I wasn't mistaken. In saying so, he was referring to the strategic plan of the creation of a Greater Serbia, a plan which he hasn't given up on. All that we've been discussing for the past two days, trying to piece together the mosaic of the developments, when we looked at the axis along which the armed rebellion spread, I believe that when one looks at all these matters, it isn't difficult to make inferences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now have a short break, a quarter-of-an-hour break, because my aim is to enable Mr. Seselj to finish his cross-examination and allow a little time for redirect, so that you don't have to come back tomorrow. So we'll have a very short break. I said a quarter-of-an-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing. So that we do not address any housekeeping matter, at a few minutes to 7.00, I would like to say straight away that the upcoming witness, the Prosecution has asked to have two and a half hours to lead this witness. Given the procedural issues, we know that the second witness to finish tomorrow's witness, we cannot finish tomorrow. Therefore, we have to carry on to next week. And tomorrow afternoon, we will finish at 7.00, and not at 6.30. The witness we are hear tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We will hear until 6.00. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness will be heard until 6.00, we shall stop at 6.00. I believe Mr. Seselj still has 20 to 25 minutes left, and as soon as Mr. Seselj's time is up, I would like the Registry to let me know, so that I can put questions to the Prosecution and understand whether there is any redirect. Theoretically, we should finish at 7.00 today, finish the cross-examination and finish the redirect today. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, I'm grateful to you for finally ranking me with Josip Broz Tito among the great Serbian joint criminal enterprise. Now the fact that you've invented the fact that the Serbs settled after the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences does not merit my attention anymore, but this is what I would like to ask you now: Do you know that the Yugoslav communist regime, at the end of World War II, expelled about half a million Germans, Fokstoiches [phoen], as they were called, from the area of Slavonia and Vojvodina? Just briefly, please, do you know or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of this fact, the Germans left during World War II, and at the beginning of the war itself, Kunta Bunt [phoen], from the area of the former Yugoslavia. I think that the process was slowed down afterwards and that those who wanted to leave did, in fact, leave during World War II or just before it broke out. I don't think there was any of that later on, but what you're telling me is the first time I hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the Croatian communist authorities, after World War II, expelled about 300.000 Italians from Istria and Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of that fact. This is the first time I hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Croats came to reside -- Croats from Western Croatia and Ninoska Krajina, Lika and so on came to take up residence in those houses?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that information is correct, because you don't know the ethnic composition of Istria. And you can ask around and then you'll see that you were wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
