utterances.text: Well, where are the 300.000 Italians, then?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fact is that World War II did lead to great migrations. You know that full well yourself. And, generally speaking, every war unfortunately resulted in processes like that, so it's little wonder that this came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said here that the refugees, Croatian refugees from Vojvodina, started to flow in at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992 from Beska, Slankamen, Ruma, and Hrtkovci, I assume, because Hrtkovci is in Ruma municipality, right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Sid and some other places. You did not speak about that in the year 2002. You did not tell the Prosecutor that then, but you this time did say something like that. But it's the date that's important, and I'm grateful to you for having told the truth there. At the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992 is what you say, and my meeting -- my rally in Hrtkovci was on the 6th of May, 1992. So the Croats started leaving Vojvodina six months before I, on behalf of the Serbian Radical Party, began striving for the principle of retortion and an exchange of population. Now, do you know that we Radicals in May made that idea public during the election campaign?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you said at that rally. Those people, the refugees who were in the process of exchanging their houses, did tell me who was exerting pressure on them, and you said yourself, the Radicals, and that this process of population exchanges was being initiated. And you should read the book called "Srem: The Bloody Wing of Croatia." I think that's what the title of the book is. Anyway, in that book, we have descriptions of various destinies and fates and how that process began. And if you read the book, then you know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I haven't read the book, and I'd be very grateful if you send me the book once you return to Slatina. Would you be so kind as to send me the book? Do you promise to do so?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. I'll see how you keep your promises. I hold you to that. Mr. Matovina, now what's the essential point as far as I'm concerned here that those Croats six months beforehand began to move out, that is to say before the Prosecution established in the indictment my involvement, my possible involvement in that matter. But these Croats started moving out only once the large mass of Croatian -- of Serb refugees from Croatia began arriving or arrived. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Because I have nothing on my screen right now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see the transcript on one of the screens there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask your question again, Mr. Seselj. This hasn't been recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It is clear to you, I assume, Mr. Matovina, that the exodus of the Croats from Vojvodina only began when a large mass of Serb refugees from Croatia arrived there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The process began to be intensified after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If there was any pressure on Croats, then that pressure objectively was because of this large mass of Serb refugees; right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you said yourself that you strove for that process and that you advocate it now as well, and certainly when those refugees arrived, the pressure was greater, and that that's when an agreement began to be made or agreements began to be made and contracts between the people, those who came in and those who wanted to leave, with respect to the exchange of property and houses and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I no longer advocate that, but I did advocate that in 1992, and that's no secret. Everything that I stated publicly, I never went back on, ever. I never denied having said something that I did, in fact, say. But the process began six months earlier, and that's the essential point as far as I'm concerned. May we have document 3 here now, please, and I want to show you a list of individuals who exchanged their property in Podravska Slatina; that is to say, Serbs from Podravska Slatina who exchanged their property with Croats from Hrtkovci. So take a look at that list now, and are any names familiar either on the Serb side or the Croat side? Can we have the whole list placed on the overhead projector, please. You see it says: "Bosko Zivkovic exchanged property with Mirko Trkulja from Hrtkovci." And then we have "Jovica Srepulja [phoen]." And you have no reason to doubt the authenticity of this document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: My associates compiled this in Hrtkovci itself, talking to the Serbs who came to settle there. So these are all the Serbs from Podravska Slatina, just from Podravska Slatina? From Podravska Slatina alone there are a lot from Grubisno Polje, where there was no war or any combat; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know people from Grubisno Polje, but I think people exchanged property there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you know that Grubisno Polje was emptied of the Serbs? I assume you know that.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many people exchanged houses and property in that area. I know about Slatina and Virovitica, Podravina, that county.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Matovina, if you say you don't know, I won't insist upon the fact. I don't want to extort confessions from you. Now, I have a statement here which Bojo Radmilovic gave. He's a Serb from Podravska Slatina, and he gave that statement to the Serbian information centre of the Serb Sabor or Assembly. And this is a copy of the statement. It's not the original. The original is in the archives of the Document and Information Centre of the Serb Assembly. The OTP cooperates with them. They probably have them. I had to find it elsewhere. But, anyway, have you heard of this man, Bojo Radmilovic?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who that is. Could you explain to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He describes here how the mining of Serb houses started in Podravska Slatina immediately after the withdrawal of the Serbs from Papuk and Psunj and the mass exodus from Western Slavonia. Up until then, there was no mining, and then he says that the mining started and that Milan Lazic's house was mined.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was mining, and I spoke about that earlier on when we discussed the problem of the killing. There was looting, there was mining, there was theft of property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: A short remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Mussemeyer. You're going to protest because you don't have the translation in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: No, I don't want to protest. What I want for the record is there is no signature and there is no stamp on this statement which the accused gave us. This is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave the source of this statement. I don't want to tender it into evidence. All I want is the witness's facts here. So it's an auxiliary instrument for me in my cross-examination, not to be tendered into evidence, so it doesn't have to have a stamp. I said that the original of this statement was in the Information Centre of the Serbian Sabor archives. The OTP knows where it can find it, and I believe it already has it in its possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know about the mining of Nikola Vejovic's house?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know exactly for each of the locations and each of the names and each of the buildings, but we did discuss that and we said that such incidents did happen and such crimes were committed, and that we energetically stood up to prevent it and prosecute it. There are written documents about this, reports sent to the prosecutor's office, investigations undertaken, and so on and so forth, and I think that we've discussed that problem at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Gojko Oljaca is?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We discussed that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. He was killed in January 1991; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, anyway, the beginning of 1991. You should know that, at least.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was the beginning of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When, then?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't know the exact date. There were quite a number of cases, lots of crimes during the war, and, anyway, there is a criminal report on the basis of which you can see the sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is a vivid example. Gojko Oljaca was the first person to be killed in the Podravska Slatina area, whether Serbs or Croats. He was the first victim that fell, and he was a Serb, and that's why his name came to be known. Was anybody killed before him?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was the first victim and what date that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that he was found dead by a wood where people did their driving examinations and driving lessons; children found him in a nylon bag?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. He was killed and thrown in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And from that time on, many Serbs fled from Podravska Slatina because they felt unsafe. Do you know about Milutin Gunjevic, he was dealt in glass in Podravska Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was from Cikote?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was another killing we discussed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was taken away after his house was searched, and two months later found dead in a wood in Medinci, and you never learned who the perpetrators were, who killed him?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The perpetrators weren't identified yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who searched his house; not the police, the para-police, the national guards corps?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't know. If we knew then we would have apprehended and identified the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Nikola Kosic is? He was the director of Jugobanka in Podravska Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one of the directors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was found dead in Orahovica, in a ditch there?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by Orahovica, but by Cadjevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was 50 years old?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A man called Petrovic who was the proprietor of a catering establishment, he was taken away. Vito Petrovic, in fact?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know about that. All right, fine. They arrested him by members of the -- or, rather, members of the Croatian Guards Corps, the ZNG arrested him. Now, of this Bojo Radmilovic, the ZNGs searched his house on the 1st of September, 1991, that is to say before the first major armed conflicts took place?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that event. Members of the ZNG were not in -- did not have the authority of the Ministry of the Interior. They had their own command, their headquarters and their services, but I don't know that they searched houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 20th of June, 1992, Zdenko Barisic arrived from Hrtkovci and suggested that he exchange his house. That's on page 2, and that's an interesting piece of information as far as I'm concerned. It says that he agreed to exchange his property, they drew up a contract, and he says all the property and all the land was stipulated, "And I gave him my house that was several storeys high and completely furnished and some land with five construction sites in Bojanci [phoen], where there are some vineyards, and in return I got an old house without any land and some old property which I had to renovate and work in. It didn't even have a concrete slab." And you said the Serbs fared better in the exchanges than the Croats, whereas the reality of it was quite the opposite. The Croats always got more property, property of greater value, than the property they left to the Serbs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this agreement and contract between these two citizens, the ones that you mention, nor during my years of service and duties did I deal with property at all and property exchanges, and the proportion and ratio in which they were exchanged, and whether some people fared better or worse than others, and whether you could always strike the right kind of deal with properties of equal value, because you know that when exchanges take place, somebody gets a better house, the other person gets a worse house. Those people who want to leave, leave, and probably fare worse. So I don't know how people fared, and it would be speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you would like to say that all those Serbs left voluntarily, whereas all the Croats left under pressure? You'd like to say that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, not quite like that. I've already presented my views.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me how much more time I have left, whether I should show another document or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please, how much time is there left?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document number 5, please, could you put that on the overhead projector and show the witness? We're not going to go through the entire document, but, anyway, this is a report compiled on the 30th of October and sent to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Dobrica Cosic. The date is 1992. It was sent by the Serb Sabor or Assembly. It is a report by the Serb assembly on the prosecution of Serbian people and ethnic cleansing in Western Slavonia by the Croatian authorities. The author of this report are Academician Pavle Ivic, the president of the Serbian Sabor, Academician Vasilije Krestic, the president of the Information Centre Council of the Serbian Assembly, and Vojin Dabic, the head of the Information Centre for Serbian Sabor or Assembly. May we have a look at page 24, I thought we'd have more time to dwell on this document. But anyway, I just would just like to look at a few conclusions made there. So in 1992, this is much before the "Blesak," the Flash Operation in Western Slavonia, namely, the territories of the municipalities of Daruvar, Grubisa Polje, Nova Gradiska, Novska, Pakrac, Orahovica, Podravska Slatina, Slavonska Pozega and Virovitica. The Croatian authorities, around the beginning of July 1991, up until mid-August 1992, ethnically completely cleansed 193 places, 183 rural settlements, and in them, upon the cessation of the armed conflicts in the Republic of Croatia, heavily damaged, demolished or burned the majority of the Serbian houses. They partially ethnically-cleansed 87 villages, but that is not a final number. Many of the ethnically partially-cleansed settlements would soon be -- will soon be ethnically clean, ethnically pure, if the International Community does not compel the authorities in the Republic of Croatia to stop the ethnic cleansing of their territory of the Serb population. During the ethnic cleansing, according to the data that has been compiled so far, 52.320 Serbs have been expelled from Western Slavonia. By the ethnic cleansing, the ethnic map of the Republic of Croatia has been changed, and thereby the project of an ethnically-pure Croatian state has been accomplished in large measure, in which, as formulated in the Croatian state programme at the end of the 19th century, there is no room for the Serbian orthodox population. You're a coalition partner with the Croatian Party of Rights, and you should know its leader is Ante Starcevic; is that right.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ante Starcevic was the greatest ideologue of anti-Serbian hate throughout the history of the Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you read his works?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you say that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What terms does he use to describe the Serbs? Does he not say that they are a dog's brew, the witches ripe for the axe?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because you did not read your ideologue. He says they're a dog's brew which is ripe for the axe, and that is also what the Serbs are for the Croatia of today, they are a dog's brewed ripe for the axe.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It is true.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All national rights are guaranteed under the constitution of the Republic of Croatia and the legal prescriptions based on the constitution for all the peoples, including the Serbian people who live in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. When you reduce the Serbs from 20 per cent to just a mere 4 to 5 per cent of the total population, now you guarantee their rights. You talked about Serbian rebels here. Did not the Croatian regime in Zagreb, Tudjman's regime, was not it an insurgent regime in relation to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to what provision of the constitution did this federal union have the right to secede?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Federal units have the right to self-determination and secession according to the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are making that up. That is not written anywhere in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a community of states, of republics that had the status of states, and in the process of gaining independence, each of them was entitled to actually exercise that right and achieve it in practice, and this was true for all the peoples in all the republics in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are making that up. Was Croatia constituted as a federal unit after World War II? When was it constituted, when was the Croatian federal unit constituted?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was when Yugoslavia was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yugoslavia was constituted in 1980, and then Croatia did not exist at that time.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are not talking about that Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So we're talking about the communist Yugoslavia. All right. Did the Croatian -- was the Croatian unit, federal unit, constituted in accordance with the will of the Croatian and Serbian people living in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always a federal unit in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the Serb people a constituent people in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was equal with all the other peoples who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please don't say stupidities. First of all, in terms of constituentness, the Serbian people was equal to the Croatian people; all the other nationalities were national minorities, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It is not up to the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and offend him. He should put questions to fact and not comment on what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you put a question. The witness answers. Do not make any comments on the answers provided by the witness. If you don't like the answer, rephrase your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the Serb people a constituent people in Croatia, according to all the constitutions from 1945 and on?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said so many times already, that it was equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are giving me an answer, and I'm not asking you that. I have to intervene. What I'm asking you is: Was it a constituent people? Say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have read the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What does that mean, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Republic of Croatia and of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and you have seen what is written in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the Serb people a constituent people in the Socialist Federal Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you already. It was an equal people with all other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you are not answering my question. Please say yes or no. There is not a third answer.

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. If you need an answer, I'll say, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it was a constituent people. Does it mean that no one can change the constitutional/legal status of Croatia without the consent of Serbs living in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this formulation which was there was not initially well phrased. Why it was entered in the constitution in such a way, I don't know, but the majority Croatian people in the Croatian state is, I believe, a constituent people with all the other peoples and minorities which live in it, and on that basis they all are entitled to every right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you abolished the status of a constituent people to the Serbs, and you proceeded to secede, and those Serbs who wished to remain in Yugoslavia were rebels to you, and who, who wanted to secede unconstitutionally were not rebels; right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We as a Croatian people have a right to create our own independent and sovereign state, and that right was exercised and it was internationally recognised. Had it not been created pursuant to the constitution, the laws and the will of the Croatian people, 96 per cent of which opted at the referendum for a Croatian independent state, then it would not have been created.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were recognised by these same people who are now -- who have recognised the independence of Kosovo and who have me on trial today. However, what you recognised with your unlawful documents doesn't mean that you were right. Where was it written? Where was this right enshrined, the right of Croatia to become an independent state?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you, in the 1974 constitution. That was, in fact, the foundation upon which the Croatian state was able to proceed with -- to embark upon the process of disassociation and that of gaining independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The moment Tudjman assumed power --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, just so you're not caught by surprise, I just wanted to inform you that you have one minute left. If you have a last question to ask, do so. You have one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the dissatisfaction of the Serbian -- did a Serbian policeman become dissatisfied when Tudjman's regime changed the markings on the cockades, when it introduced the Ustasha checkered flag instead of the earlier five-star-pointed flag?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons, but it shouldn't have been that way, because it is not a cockade, it is a historical coat of arms of Croatia which was only established by the Croatian Assembly with certain changes thereto. And why wouldn't that be a mark to be worn by the Croatian police if we do have an independent and autonomous state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Tudjman introduce the Ustasha currency called kuna? Was the kuna ever in use as a currency -- as a monetary unit in Croatia before the Ustasha regime of Ante Pavelic?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the kuna is not a Ustasha currency. It is the currency of the independent Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was the currency used in the Ustasha state during the Second World War and then in Tudjman's date. Never in any other period in history did such a currency exist in Croatia. Only during Ante Pavelic and Tudjman's regimes; right?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did it exist, in what other period?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a historic Croatian currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are inventing things. The Croats never had that currency in history. That was in Slavonia, just as the Slavonia Dinar, the so-called Banovac in one period in history, and the Croatians never had any other currency until Pavelic's time. You don't even know Croatian history. I have to give you lessons?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, of course I do. You're exaggerating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is well, tell me, when was the kuna currency before Pavelic, which ruler, in which period was that?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's not go into historical waters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you contend that this was the case, but you don't know when, and you are ready to affirm this fact. This is how much you care for the truth. As my minute is up, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, your time is up. Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I ask myself: Where is the relevance to this case, it's monetary currency of Croat today, and former times where's the relevance to this case? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I explain this to Mr. Mussemeyer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, before I give the floor to the Prosecutor for the redirect, I wanted to ask you: The independence of Croatia and its international recognition took place in 1992; you agree with that? Okay. In 1991, it was still former Yugoslavia; you agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did exist, but the Croatian Assembly adopted the constitution and documents on this, disassociation, and the declaration on the severance of all constitution and legal connections with the former state, a declaration proclaiming the JNA an enemy army, and in that process, at the request of the International Community, the process was prolonged or postponed. And after its recognition on the 15th of January, 1992, Croatia became an independent and sovereign state recognised by the world. But these documents, all these constitution and legal documents, had been adopted prior to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said the same thing yesterday, but I let you go on. In 1991, what was the legal currency in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Yugoslavia, the official currency was the dinar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, it was the dinar. In Croatia, at what point in time did the kuna appear, from your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, there was the Croatian dinar, and the kuna was introduced later. I believe that was in the 1990s, after these war developments were over. The Croatian dinar was the first currency introduced after the dinar. I'm not quite sure of the exact date when the Croatian dinar was actually substituted for the kuna. It was far after these events that we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So the Croatian dinar, when did it occur; in 1992, 1991, 1990? When did it occur?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that happened already in 1991 or in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how did it happen? When you had Yugoslav dinars, did you bring them to the bank and receive Croatian dinars in exchange?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We had an exchange of currencies, and the Croatian dinar was in circulation and was used in commerce and trade and in various transactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Mr. Mussemeyer for redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: There is no need for redirect. I have only two issues on the record. For one, I need the witness. For the other one, I don't need him. The first one refers to page 44, line 7. I think there is a mistake. Let me go there. The witness was asked by Judge Harhoff: "When did the witness stop working?" And then his answer was: "The year 2000." And I think it was the witness said: "1971." I would like to have the witness confirming this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was when I started working in the police, so I started working on the 18th of June, 1971, and it ended on the 1st of January, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. I have no further questions where I need the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, Witness, I thank you on behalf of my colleagues for coming to give your evidence for the OTP here. So you can now go back to your country. I will ask the usher to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, distinguished Bench, everyone in the courtroom. Thank you very much. I wish you good luck and good health. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give you the floor, Mr. Mussemeyer, I would like to thank the interpreters, who are doing wonders to translate almost in realtime what the accused and the witness are saying. Today, as I'm speaking to you at 6.48 and 18 seconds, we have almost 109 pages of transcript. That's a record, so our interpreters are really doing wonders. I wanted to thank them, even though sometimes there might be some mistakes. But given the speed, it's quite understandable. Mr. Mussemeyer, what would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: My second issue refers to page 24, line 8. The witness has been asked when the accused's name has been mentioned the first time, and he answered: "No." Then the accused, Mr. Seselj, says: "That's a very important piece of information for me, and I want to corroborate that by the fact that according to what Carla Del Ponte said, it was in 2002 that the prime minister, Djindjic, ordered that I be arrested and extradited." This is not correct. I checked the book of Madam Del Ponte, where she is referring to her conversation with Mr. Djindjic, and it was not in 2002. It was the 17th of February, 2003, a date when the indictment against the accused has already been approved. I mention this because it has to be on the record, that Mr. Seselj cannot always insinuate a conspiracy. At least the dates should be corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, wait a minute before giving you the floor. I was forgetting somebody else, but it goes without saying that court reporters are also doing wondering, and we have a beautiful transcript in realtime as well. So, of course, it goes without saying, so I forgot to say so. I forgot to thank him, but I want to tell the Court reporter that he's also doing wondering, and thanks to him we can follow all the statements in realtime. Mr. Seselj, what did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know what it says in your transcript, but I said that Zoran Djindjic ordered my arrest or instructed that I be arrested, not ordered. These are two different expressions in Serbian. How this is being interpreted, I don't know. "Commissioned my arrest," if you like. Now, Mrs. [Indiscernible] talks about Carla Del Ponte in her facts, says that it wasn't 2002 but 2003. Anyway, it was before Mr. Mussemeyer -- it was before I came to The Hague, and I'm happy that you've read Carla Del Ponte's book. I still haven't, because I haven't got it. I was just able to read the excerpts published in the Serbian press, but I think that -- I hope that the Trial Chamber will state its views with respect to what Carla Del Ponte says and the role of Zoran Djindjic in my arrest and this whole rigged legal proceedings on me that is falling flat through each subsequent witness. There is no expert on whom the Prosecution could be satisfied with and who will bear out even a single letter of the indictment, and that is there's a crash in the whole proceedings because the whole trial was rigged and is rigged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trumped up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have the time to read the whole book, but I read the relevant part, and that is on page 187, where Madam Del Ponte was referring to this, and the reason I mention this was the date. The date should be corrected. It was the 17th of February, 2003, and not in 2002. It was a date after the indictment had already been approved. Mr. Seselj is right, he wasn't here at that time, but I wanted to put this straight. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an invention that the indictment was confirmed in 2002. The indictment was confirmed only in 2003, and I learnt that an indictment had been raised against me through my man who's working for the Prosecution even to this day, before it was disclosed. And when, on the 25th of January, I stated that there was an indictment prepared against me, everybody denied it, until Carla Del Ponte came to Belgrade and brought the indictment with her, and she did that sometime in mid-February. But, anyway, on the 25th of January, I bought a plane ticket for The Hague, and the indictment was brought to Belgrade only in mid-February. I had to reserve an airline flight, because you know planes from Belgrade are full all the time, and I wanted to fly in a Serb plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, the indictment must have been confirmed in 2003 and not in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I apologise if I should have mentioned the wrong year. It's correct, it has been approved in January of 2003. This is my recollection. I can't give you the exact date, but it was in January of 2003. So what Mr. Seselj says about the 25th of January may be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then, as I said, we'll have tomorrow's witness tomorrow. The Prosecution planned two hours and a half. Given the many problems and Judges' questions, we will not be able to finish by tomorrow. Mr. Seselj will also have two hours and a half for cross-examination. The hearing tomorrow will stop at 6.00, and we'll resume the hearing of the witness Tuesday from 8.30 onwards. That's it for the schedule. If there are no further questions, I will adjourn the meeting, and we will resume tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of May, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.56 p.m.,
